prompt: By about what year had Rome become a city?
explanation: Rome grew from farming villages on seven hills by the River Tiber and was a city by 753 BC.

prompt: Why did the Romans throw out King Tarquin in 509 BC?
options: He lost a war with Carthage
explanation: Tarquin was a tyrant, so the Romans got rid of him and Rome became a republic.

prompt: Who ran the Roman Republic?
options: One king chosen by the gods
Two elected consuls advised by the Senate
explanation: In the republic two consuls were elected, and the Senate advised them.

prompt: Why did consuls serve for only one year and have to agree on decisions?
options: Because the Senate was too busy
explanation: Short terms and shared power made it hard for one man to become corrupt or too powerful.

prompt: Who became the first Roman emperor in 27 BC?
explanation: Octavian took the name Augustus Caesar and became the first emperor in 27 BC.

prompt: How was the huge Roman Empire run?
options: It was split into provinces run by governors
Each town elected its own king
explanation: The empire was divided into provinces, and each one had a governor.

prompt: What buried Pompeii and Herculaneum in AD 79?
options: A flood from the River Tiber
explanation: Mount Vesuvius erupted and covered both towns in about six metres of ash and rock.

prompt: How do archaeologists show what Pompeii victims looked like in their last moments?
options: They study paintings of the eruption
They pour plaster into hollows left by the bodies
They read letters written by victims
They use X-rays on the ash
explanation: The bodies left hollows in the hardened ash. Plaster poured in makes a cast of the person.

prompt: What were rich Roman nobles and landowners called?
explanation: Patricians were the small group of rich nobles. Plebeians were the poor majority.

prompt: What was a domus?
options: The house of a rich family
explanation: A domus was a rich family's private house, with an atrium, garden and heating.

prompt: Which of these describes an insulae?
options: A country villa with a garden
Apartment blocks where plebeians rented rooms
explanation: Insulae were blocks up to five storeys high. They often burned or fell down.

prompt: Why were the upper floors of an insulae cheaper?
options: They had no water and were hard to escape in a fire
explanation: Upper floors had no water and were the most dangerous, so the rent was lower.

prompt: What was the cena?
options: The main meal of the day
explanation: Cena was the main meal. Rich Romans ate it lying on couches.

prompt: What was the dole in ancient Rome?
options: Free grain given to the poor
explanation: The government gave free grain, called the dole, to poor Romans.

prompt: What did a male Roman citizen wear over his tunic?
explanation: Male citizens wore a toga. Married women wore a stola.

prompt: What did boys learn at grammar school from age twelve?
explanation: Oratory was important because rich young men might become lawyers or politicians.

prompt: Where did Romans go to watch chariot racing?
explanation: The Circus Maximus held up to 250,000 fans for chariot races.

prompt: What were gladiators?
options: Trained fighters who battled each other or animals
explanation: Gladiators fought in public shows, for example in the Colosseum.

prompt: In what order did Romans use the rooms at the baths?
options: Cold room, hot room, warm room
Warm room, hot room, cold room
Hot room, cold room, warm room
Cold room, warm room, hot room
explanation: They went from the warm room to the hot room and finished in the cold room.

prompt: What is polytheism?
explanation: The Romans were polytheists. They worshipped many gods, such as Jupiter and Mars.

prompt: Where did early Christians in Rome bury their dead?
explanation: Christians were persecuted, so they buried their dead in underground tunnels called catacombs.

prompt: What was decimation in the Roman army?
options: Every tenth soldier in a cohort was executed
Soldiers were paid every ten days
Soldiers marched ten miles a day
explanation: Decimation was a harsh punishment: one soldier in every ten was killed.

prompt: What did a soldier get after 25 years in the army?
explanation: After 25 years' service a legionary got a final payment and land.

prompt: What was manumission?
explanation: Manumission was the ceremony where a slave was set free.

prompt: What was a dowry in Roman times?
options: Money or goods the bride's family gave
explanation: Marriages were arranged and the bride's family gave a dowry.

prompt: Which of these is a Roman achievement we still use today?
explanation: Roman numerals and the names of our months come from Rome. Latin also grew into Italian, Spanish and French.

prompt: Say in your own words: how did Rome go from a monarchy to a republic to an empire?
model_answer: Rome was first ruled by seven kings. In 509 BC the Romans threw out the tyrant Tarquin and set up a republic run by two elected consuls and the Senate. In 27 BC Octavian (Augustus) became the first emperor.

prompt: Say in your own words: why are Pompeii and Herculaneum so important to historians?
model_answer: Vesuvius buried both towns in ash in AD 79, so streets, shops, houses, mosaics and artefacts were preserved. Plaster casts even show people in their last moments. This tells us a lot about everyday Roman life.

prompt: Explain the difference between a domus and an insulae.
model_answer: A domus was the private house of a rich family, with an atrium, garden, heating and running water. An insulae was a crowded apartment block where poor plebeians rented rooms. Insulae often caught fire or collapsed.

prompt: Describe education in ancient Rome.
model_answer: Only children of rich families went to school, from age seven, to learn reading, writing and sums with an abacus and wax tablets. At twelve, boys went to grammar school to learn oratory. Girls stayed at home to prepare for marriage, and poor children did not go to school.

prompt: Say in your own words: how did Romans enjoy themselves?
model_answer: They watched chariot racing at the Circus Maximus and gladiators at the Colosseum. They went to the public baths, moving from the warm room to the hot room to the cold room. They also went to the theatre.

prompt: Explain the difference between polytheism and monotheism, using Rome as an example.
model_answer: Polytheism means worshipping many gods, like the Romans did with Jupiter, Juno and Mars. Monotheism means believing in one god, like the early Christians. Christians were persecuted until Emperor Constantine became a Christian.

prompt: Describe the life of a Roman legionary.
model_answer: Legionaries marched 20 miles a day carrying weapons, tools and food. They wore helmets and armour and fought with short swords and spears. Discipline was harsh, and after 25 years they got a payment and land.

prompt: Give three ways the Romans still affect our lives today.
model_answer: They first made concrete and built roads, and Roman-style buildings like the GPO still copy their domes and pillars. Latin grew into Italian, Spanish and French, and we still use Roman numerals and month names. Rome also became the home of the Catholic Church.

prompt:
(e) Name the ancient or medieval civilisation you studied for your Junior Cycle History course. Describe three important achievements of the civilisation you studied.
Name of ancient or medieval civilisation:
Achievements:
(f) In your opinion, which of these achievements had the greatest impact on later history? Explain your answer.
model_answer:
(e) Civilisation: Ancient Rome.
1. Roads and building: the Romans first made concrete and built a huge network of stone roads, starting with the Appian Way. Armies, traders and messages could travel quickly across the empire. They also built aqueducts to bring clean water to cities.
2. Language: the Romans spoke Latin, which spread across the empire. Latin grew into Italian, Spanish and French, and we still use Roman numerals and the Roman names of the months.
3. Law: the Twelve Tables were written laws put up in the Forum so everyone could see them. This meant the law was the same for everyone and could not just be made up by a ruler.
(f) I think the Latin language had the greatest impact. Long after the empire fell, Latin was still used by the Church and by scholars all over Europe. It grew into Italian, Spanish and French, which millions of people speak today, and many English words come from Latin too. Roads and buildings wore away, but the language lived on.
marking_scheme:
(e) Name of civilisation: 3 marks. Three achievements, 3 marks each (9 marks), on a sliding scale: 3 = very good, 2 = good/fair, 1 = poor, 0 = no merit. An achievement named without description = 1 mark max. Total 12 marks.
(f) Marked as a whole out of 6: 6 = excellent, 4 = good/very good, 2 = poor/fair, 0 = no merit. Must pick one achievement and justify it in the light of later events. An achievement named without explanation = 1 mark max.

prompt:
Read this extract from a letter by Pliny the Younger, c. AD 106, describing the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79:
"You could hear the shrieks of women, the wailing of infants, and the shouting of men; some were calling their parents, others their children or their wives, trying to recognize them by their voices."
(a) Give evidence from the source that shows people were terrified.
(b) Mention one weakness of a letter as a source.
(c) Explain how archaeology at Pompeii has helped historians learn about Roman life.
model_answer:
(a) You could hear "the shrieks of women, the wailing of infants, and the shouting of men". People were calling out for their families in the dark.
(b) A letter gives only one person's point of view, so it may be biased. Pliny also wrote it about 27 years later, so he may not remember everything correctly.
(c) The ash preserved Pompeii, so archaeologists found streets, shops, temples, mosaics and everyday artefacts. These show us how Romans lived, worked and ate. Plaster casts show the victims in their last moments.
marking_scheme:
(a) 3 marks: one piece of evidence quoted or referred to from the source.
(b) 3 marks: one valid weakness, e.g. one person's view / may be biased or exaggerated / written years later / memory may be wrong.
(c) 6 marks: two points at 3 marks each, e.g. buildings preserved, artefacts found, food and shops, plaster casts of victims.

prompt:
Using your knowledge of ancient Rome, write about the lives of people in Rome using at least two of the following themes:
(a) Housing (b) Food and drink (c) Clothes (d) Leisure and entertainment (e) Religion.
model_answer:
(a) Housing: rich patricians lived in a domus, with an atrium and pool, a garden, underfloor heating, running water and mosaics. Poor plebeians rented rooms in insulae, apartment blocks up to five storeys high made of timber and mud brick. Insulae often burned or collapsed, and the upper floors had no water.
(b) Food and drink: rich Romans ate three meals a day. The main meal, cena, had several courses served by slaves, and they ate lying on couches. Poor Romans ate bread, porridge, beans and lentils, bought hot food at thermopolia, and got free grain from the government, called the dole.
(d) Leisure and entertainment: Romans watched chariot racing at the Circus Maximus, where up to 250,000 fans cheered. At the Colosseum, which held 70,000, gladiators fought each other or wild animals. People also went to the public baths, moving from the warm room to the hot room to the cold room.
marking_scheme: Marked like a 'people in history' answer: 3 marks for each relevant, developed point (a key point or a development of a point with new information), up to about 18 marks, plus marks for overall organisation. At least two themes must be covered; one theme only = about two-thirds of the marks max.

prompt: How did Christianity probably first reach Ireland, before AD 400?
options: Through traders and slaves from Roman Britain and Gaul
Through Irish monks returning from Iona
explanation: Traders and slaves from Roman Britain and Gaul probably brought Christianity before AD 400.

prompt: Who sent Palladius to Ireland as a bishop in AD 431?
explanation: Pope Celestine I sent Palladius in AD 431. We know little about what happened to him.

prompt: How did St Patrick first come to Ireland?
options: As a bishop sent by the Pope
He was captured by pirates and sold as a slave
explanation: At sixteen Patrick was captured by pirates and sold as a slave in Ireland, where he herded sheep.

prompt: What is the name of the book in which St Patrick tells his own story?
explanation: Patrick wrote about his life in his Confession. It is a primary source.

prompt: Why did St Patrick try to convert Gaelic chieftains first?
options: If a chieftain converted, his whole clan would too
Only chieftains were allowed in churches
explanation: When a chief became Christian, his people usually followed him.

prompt: What is a diocese?
options: The area controlled by a bishop
explanation: Patrick set up dioceses, and each one was run by a bishop.

prompt: Where did nuns live?
explanation: Monks lived in monasteries and nuns lived in convents.

prompt: What does it mean that monasteries were self-sufficient?
options: They were paid by the king
They grew their own food and made their own clothes
explanation: Monks and nuns produced what they needed themselves, so they did not rely on others.

prompt: Who set up a convent in Kildare?
explanation: St Brigid set up her convent in Kildare in about AD 470.

prompt: Which monastery is 12 km off the coast of Kerry, where monks lived in beehive huts?
explanation: Skellig Michael was founded by St Fionán on a rocky island off Kerry.

prompt: Who founded Clonmacnoise?
explanation: St Ciarán founded Clonmacnoise in Co. Offaly in AD 549.

prompt: Who founded Glendalough in Co. Wicklow?
explanation: St Kevin founded the monastery at Glendalough.

prompt: Why was Ireland called the 'land of saints and scholars'?
options: Some monasteries were like universities and people came to learn
Every Irish person became a monk
explanation: Monasteries like Clonmacnoise were great centres of learning, and visitors came from abroad.

prompt: What was the oratory in a monastery?
explanation: The oratory was a small church where monks prayed.

prompt: In which building did monks eat their meals?
explanation: Meals were eaten in the refectory.

prompt: Why was the door of a round tower high above the ground?
options: So bells could be rung through it
So monks could pull up the ladder during an attack
explanation: A high door reached by a ladder made the tower a safer store and lookout during raids.

prompt: What was a tonsure?
options: The shaved crown of a monk's head
explanation: Monks shaved the crown of their heads. This was called a tonsure.

prompt: What did scribes write on?
explanation: Scribes wrote on vellum (calfskin) or parchment (sheepskin), using a goose-feather quill.

prompt: Where is the Book of Kells kept today?
explanation: The Book of Kells, a copy of the four gospels, is in Trinity College Dublin.

prompt: What did high crosses show?
explanation: High crosses showed Bible stories and marked the centre of a monastery or an important grave.

prompt: What is filigree?
options: Weaving thin gold and silver threads into patterns
explanation: Metalworkers used filigree on objects like the Ardagh Chalice.

prompt: Where did St Colmcille set up a monastery in AD 563?
explanation: Colmcille founded a monastery on the island of Iona in Scotland.

prompt: Which Irish monk founded monasteries at Luxeuil in France and Bobbio in Italy?
explanation: St Columbanus helped keep Christianity alive in Europe after Rome fell.

prompt: In what year did Viking raids on Ireland begin?
explanation: The Vikings first raided the Irish coast in AD 795.

prompt: Which of these towns did the Vikings found?
explanation: The Vikings founded seaport towns such as Dublin, Waterford and Wexford.

prompt: Which pagan festival became St Brigid's Day?
explanation: The pagan festival of Imbolc became the Christian feast of St Brigid's Day.

prompt: Say in your own words: what did St Patrick do to spread Christianity in Ireland?
model_answer: After escaping slavery and training as a priest in France, Patrick returned in AD 432. He baptised pagans, built churches and set up dioceses run by bishops. He converted chieftains so their whole clan would follow.

prompt: Explain why monks and nuns chose to live in monasteries and convents.
model_answer: They wanted to give their lives to God through prayer and work. They chose quiet, isolated places away from distractions. They lived by strict rules of obedience, poverty and chastity.

prompt: Give two uses of a round tower.
model_answer: A round tower was a bell tower that called monks to prayer. It was also a lookout and a safe store for valuables during raids, with a high door reached by a ladder.

prompt: Describe the daily life of a monk in Early Christian Ireland.
model_answer: A monk followed strict rules, with set times to rise, pray, eat and sleep. Many monks were farmers, and some were scribes in the scriptorium. He wore a simple woollen tunic, a hooded cape and sandals, and had a tonsure.

prompt: Say in your own words: how were manuscripts made?
model_answer: Scribes in the scriptorium copied the Bible and lives of saints by hand. They wrote on vellum with a goose-feather quill, using ink made from plants and powdered coloured stones. The Book of Kells is the most famous example.

prompt: Describe two kinds of art made in Early Christian monasteries.
model_answer: Stonemasons carved high crosses with Bible stories, such as Muiredach's Cross at Monasterboice. Metalworkers used filigree to make objects like the Ardagh Chalice and the Derrynaflan Chalice.

prompt: Explain how the Vikings affected Ireland.
model_answer: From AD 795 Vikings raided monasteries, taking gold and silver and kidnapping people as slaves. This led to the decline of the monasteries. But they also founded towns like Dublin, Waterford and Wexford and later became Christian.

prompt: Say in your own words: why does Early Christian Ireland still matter today?
model_answer: The diocese and church structure set up then still exists. Pagan festivals became Christian ones, like St Brigid's Day. Many towns began around monasteries, and ruins like Glendalough are part of our heritage.

model_answer:
(ii) I am a monk at Clonmacnoise, a monastery founded by St Ciarán beside the River Shannon. There were also famous monasteries at Glendalough, Kells and Skellig Michael.
I became a monk because I wanted to give my life to God. I promised to live in poverty, chastity and obedience, and I wear a simple woollen tunic, a hooded cape and sandals. The crown of my head is shaved in a tonsure.
Our day follows strict rules. We rise very early and stop work many times to pray together in the oratory, a small stone church. We eat simple food in the refectory, mostly bread, vegetables, milk and fish. Our monastery is self-sufficient: many monks farm the land and grow our food.
I work in the scriptorium as a scribe. I copy the gospels by hand onto vellum, made from calfskin, using a quill made from a goose feather. Our ink comes from plants and crushed coloured stones, and we decorate the first letters with bright colours.
Clonmacnoise is a great centre of learning. Students come from Ireland and abroad to learn to read and write in Latin and Irish. Sick people are cared for in our infirmary, and guests stay in the guesthouse.
Our round tower is a bell tower and a lookout. Its door is high off the ground. When the Vikings raid, we climb in with our books and gold chalices and pull up the ladder behind us.

prompt: Say in your own words: how did the feudal system work?

prompt: Name two dangers of living in a medieval town and explain why they happened.

prompt: Explain what the Black Death was and what it did to Europe.

prompt:
Archaeology students at University College Dublin (UCD) built a medieval round house based on an 8th century house uncovered during excavations in Co. Antrim. Look at the sources below and answer the questions which follow.
Source 1: Photographs of the UCD medieval round house.
[Picture: Two photographs: the outside of the round house, and the inside with a fire]
Source 2: Information about the UCD medieval round house.
- The house required 250 vertical hazel posts, 1,600 horizontal hazel rods, 4 oak timbers for the doorway, 4 oak planks for the door, 1.5 tonnes of heather for the roof, and lots of grass, moss, bracken and weeds to line the walls.
- If the outside temperature was 8°, the inside temperature could be 18-21°, but the temperature dropped fast if the fire went out. Smoke drifted out through the roof. Carbon sensors recorded smoke pollution inside the house as quite low but the house stank.
- The house was alive with beetles, spiders, woodlice, birds and even a pygmy shrew. Archaeological evidence from Co. Antrim indicates that the beds would have been warm and dry but full of lice.
(a) Which of the following years are in the 8th century? Tick one of the following: 700s AD / 800s AD / 900s AD
(b) If you were an archaeology student, what would you learn from the experience of building and using the round house? Use evidence from the sources to support your answer.
(c) What are three differences between a medieval round house and a typical house or apartment in Ireland today? Refer to the sources in your answer.
model_answer:
(a) 700s AD.
(b) 1. Building it took a huge amount of natural material: 250 hazel posts, 1,600 hazel rods and 1.5 tonnes of heather for the roof. I would learn that people needed lots of work and local materials to build a home.
2. The house was warm, 18-21° inside when it was 8° outside, but only while the fire was lit. I would learn that the fire had to be kept going all the time.
3. The house stank and was full of beetles, spiders and woodlice, and the beds were full of lice. I would learn that life was dirty and uncomfortable, which could spread disease.
(c) 1. Heating: the round house was heated by an open fire on the floor and smoke drifted out through the roof. Today homes have chimneys or central heating, so there is no smoke inside.
2. Materials: the round house was made of hazel rods, oak and a heather roof. Today houses are built of concrete blocks, glass and slate or tiles.
3. Cleanliness: the round house was full of insects, birds and even a shrew, and the beds had lice. Today homes are much cleaner, with bathrooms and running water.

prompt: (d) Explain the aspects of medieval life which lowered average life expectancy during medieval times.
model_answer:
(d) In 1350 life expectancy was only about 30-40 years, for several reasons.
1. Dirty towns: towns had no sewers, and rubbish was thrown into the streets. Diseases spread easily.
2. The Black Death: this plague, spread by fleas on rats, killed about one-third of Europe's people after 1347.
3. Poor medicine: doctors followed Galen's old ideas and had no way to cure infections, so even small wounds could kill.
4. Childbirth: having a baby was very dangerous, and many mothers and babies died.
5. Poor diet and hunger: peasants lived mainly on bread and pottage, and a bad harvest could mean starvation.
6. War: knights and soldiers were often killed in battles and sieges.
marking_scheme: (d) 3 marks per key point or development, up to 15 marks (5 points). Could refer to: lack of hygiene, disease / Black Death, famine / poor diet, deaths in childbirth, high infant and child deaths, poor medical care, warfare.

THE MIDDLE AGES

model_answer:
(i) Chapter house: the room where monks met to discuss the business of the monastery.
Cloister: a covered walkway around a garden in the middle of the monastery, where monks walked and prayed.
(ii) Page: at seven, a boy was sent to another lord's castle. He learned to ride, use a sword, read and have good manners, and served the lord and lady.
Squire: at fourteen he practised archery and fighting on horseback. He went into battle with his lord and cared for his horse and weapons.
Dubbing: at twenty-one he knelt before his lord, swore an oath of chivalry and was tapped on the shoulder with a sword. He was now a knight.
(iii) (a) A serf on a medieval manor: I am a serf on Lord Hugh's manor. I am not free: I cannot leave the manor or marry without his permission. I must work free on his land, the demesne, for part of each week. I farm my own strips in the three big fields, and each year one field is left fallow. I pay a tithe, one-tenth of my crops, to the Church. The bailiff watches our work and collects the rent. My family lives in a wattle-and-daub house with a thatched roof and a hole for the smoke. We eat bread and pottage and drink ale, because the water is dirty.
(c) The training of a medieval craftsman: I am a shoemaker in Kilkenny. At twelve I became an apprentice and lived with my master for seven years. I got food and a bed but no pay while I learned the trade. Then I became a journeyman and could get paid work with other masters. To become a master craftsman I made a masterpiece, a fine pair of boots, and showed it to the shoemakers' guild. Now I can open my own shop. The guild sets our prices and wages, keeps standards high and helps members who are sick.

prompt:
From your knowledge of medieval times, write an account of life and/or death in a medieval setting of your choice: a medieval manor, a medieval town, a medieval castle, or another medieval setting.
Write about at least two of these topics: living conditions; working life; leisure; defending the settlement; religion; illness and death.
model_answer:
Setting: a medieval town.
Living conditions: houses were made of wood with thatched roofs and built close together. There were no sewers, so rubbish and waste were thrown into the streets. A bell rang at sunset for curfew, when all fires and candles had to be put out.
Working life: craftsmen belonged to guilds, which set prices and wages and kept standards high. A boy started as an apprentice at twelve, became a journeyman and could become a master craftsman by making a masterpiece.
Defending the settlement: the town had stone walls and gates. Traders paid a toll at the gate, and the gates were closed at night.
Illness and death: dirty streets helped diseases spread. In 1347 the Black Death arrived, spread by fleas on rats, and killed about one-third of Europe's people.
marking_scheme: 3 marks for each relevant, developed point, up to about 18 marks, plus marks for overall organisation. Must name a medieval setting and cover at least two of the topics.

prompt: Say in your own words: why did the Renaissance begin in Italy?
model_answer: Roman ruins reminded Italians of a glorious past. Greek scholars fled to Italy with ancient texts after Constantinople fell in 1453. Rich city-states competed for the best art, and wealthy merchants and popes could pay artists as patrons.

prompt: Explain what a patron was and give one example.
model_answer: A patron was a wealthy person who paid artists and writers to create work. For example, Pope Julius II paid Michelangelo to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling.

prompt: Describe three ways Renaissance painting was different from medieval painting.
model_answer: Renaissance painters used perspective to give depth, and sfumato to blend colours softly. They used oil paint on canvas, which allowed more detail. They painted real faces, emotions and ordinary people, not just Bible stories.

prompt: Describe the achievements of Leonardo da Vinci.
model_answer: Leonardo painted The Last Supper, which shows expert perspective, and the Mona Lisa, which uses sfumato. He drew anatomy from about 30 dissections. His notebooks also had ideas for inventions like a flying machine.

prompt: Explain why the printing press was so important.
model_answer: Gutenberg's movable type made books much cheaper to produce. More people could buy books and learn to read. Renaissance ideas spread quickly across Europe.

prompt: Describe the work of William Shakespeare.
model_answer: Shakespeare wrote comedies, tragedies such as Macbeth and Romeo and Juliet, and histories. He also wrote 154 sonnets. His company, the King's Men, built the Globe theatre in London in 1599.

prompt: Say in your own words: how did ideas about the universe change during the Renaissance?
model_answer: People had believed Ptolemy's idea that the Earth was at the centre. Copernicus said the Earth goes around the sun. Galileo's telescope proved him right, and Kepler showed the planets move in ellipses.

prompt: Describe two changes in medicine during the Renaissance.
model_answer: Vesalius wrote the first detailed anatomy textbook in 1543, based on dissections. Paré tied ligatures to close wounds instead of burning them, and treated gunshot wounds with a gentler mixture.

(iii) William Shakespeare was the most famous writer of the Renaissance. He was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in England in 1564 and moved to London, where he became an actor and playwright.

prompt: Describe Portugal's part in the Age of Exploration.
model_answer: Prince Henry planned voyages down the west coast of Africa from Sagres. Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488. Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in India in 1498, giving Portugal a sea route to Asia.

prompt: Describe Columbus's first voyage.
model_answer: Columbus left Palos on 3 August 1492 with the Santa Maria, the Pinta and the Niña, paid for by Ferdinand and Isabella. He kept two logbooks so the crew would not panic. On 12 October he landed in the Bahamas, met the Taíno and thought he was in India.

prompt: Say in your own words: what happened on Magellan's voyage?
model_answer: Magellan sailed west for Spain in 1519 to find a route to the Spice Islands. He found the Strait of Magellan, but many sailors died of scurvy crossing the Pacific, and he was killed in the Philippines. Elcano brought the Victoria home in 1522: the first ship to sail round the world.

prompt: Describe the conquest of the Aztecs.
model_answer: In 1519 Cortés landed in Mexico with 600 men, cannons, horses and dogs, and burned his ships. He captured Montezuma II, who was later killed. With native allies he besieged Tenochtitlán, which fell after three months and became Mexico City.

prompt: Describe the conquest of the Incas.
model_answer: In 1531 Pizarro set out with 180 men and trapped the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca. Atahualpa filled a room with gold and silver for his release, but the Spanish executed him. Pizarro took Cuzco, and up to 90 per cent of the Incas died of smallpox.

prompt: Explain how the Age of Exploration affected native peoples.
model_answer: Millions died from diseases like smallpox and from violence. Many were forced to become Christian or were enslaved, and the Aztec and Inca civilisations were destroyed. African slaves were then shipped in to work on plantations.

prompt:
SOURCE E: Bartolomé de las Casas, A Brief Account of the Devastation of the Indies
Of all the people of the world, the Indians are naturally the most patient and peaceful. They hold no grudges and do not start fights ... They are ready and willing to learn, so it is very likely they will accept our Catholic religion and our virtuous customs.
Yet into these sheep came some Spaniards who immediately behaved like wild wolves. The Spaniards killed and terrorised the native peoples in order to gain more gold and to make themselves richer. With their horses and metal weapons, the Spaniards began to carry out massacres and strange cruelties against Indians ...

prompt:
Write an account of one of the following:
(i) The contribution of Portugal to the Age of Exploration.
(ii) The conquest of Mexico.
(iii) The conquest of Peru.
model_answer:
(iii) The conquest of Peru.
Reasons for the conquest: the Spanish wanted gold and silver, land for Spain and to spread Christianity. They had heard of the rich Inca empire in Peru.
Pizarro and the Incas: in 1531 Francisco Pizarro, a conquistador, set out to conquer Peru with only 180 men. The Spanish had horses, guns and steel swords, which the Incas had never seen.
Meeting Atahualpa: Pizarro met the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca and trapped him there.
Atahualpa imprisoned: Atahualpa offered to fill a room with gold and silver to be set free, and his people did so.
Death of Atahualpa: even after the ransom was paid, the Spanish executed him in 1533.
Consequences: Pizarro went on to capture Cuzco, the Inca capital. Up to 90 per cent of the Inca people died of smallpox. The Inca civilisation was destroyed, natives were forced to become Christian, and gold and silver were shipped to Spain.

prompt: Did the Age of Exploration do more harm than good? Give at least two arguments for each side, then give your own verdict.

model_answer: Some clergy gave jobs to relatives (nepotism), sold Church jobs (simony) or held several jobs and were never in their parish (pluralism and absenteeism). Some popes lived in luxury, and many priests were poorly educated. The sale of indulgences seemed to make forgiveness something you could buy.

prompt: Explain why Luther objected to indulgences.
model_answer: Indulgences were certificates sold to shorten a soul's time in purgatory. Luther believed forgiveness could not be bought and that the Church was using people's fear to make money. He believed only genuine faith in God could save you.

prompt: Describe what happened in 1517.
model_answer: Johann Tetzel sold indulgences in Saxony to pay for rebuilding St Peter's Basilica. Luther wrote 95 complaints, the 95 Theses, and legend says he nailed them to the Castle Church door in Wittenberg on 31 October. The printing press spread them quickly across Germany.

prompt: Say in your own words: what happened at the Diet of Worms?
model_answer: In 1521 Emperor Charles V called Luther to the Diet of Worms and asked him to recant. Luther refused, saying 'Here I stand. I can do no other.' The Edict of Worms made him an outlaw, and Prince Frederick hid him in Wartburg Castle.

prompt: Give three differences between Catholic and Lutheran beliefs.
model_answer: Catholics believed in prayer, good deeds and confession; Lutherans believed in justification by faith alone. Catholics had seven sacraments; Lutherans kept two. Catholics used Latin and their clergy could not marry; Lutherans used the vernacular and their clergy could marry.

prompt: Describe how Protestantism spread beyond Germany.
model_answer: John Calvin set up a church in Geneva with strict rules, and he believed in predestination. In England, Henry VIII made himself head of the Church of England with the Act of Supremacy in 1534, and he closed the monasteries.

prompt: Describe two ways the Catholic Church responded to the Reformation.
model_answer: The Council of Trent (1545-1563) ended abuses like simony and pluralism and made priests train in seminaries. Ignatius Loyola founded the Jesuits, who spread the Catholic faith. The Inquisition tried heretics and the Index banned books.

prompt: Explain how the Reformation still affects Europe today.
model_answer: Europe was divided into a mainly Protestant north and Catholic south. The Bible was translated into everyday languages, which improved literacy. The Catholic Church reformed itself, and the Pope lost power in Protestant countries.

model_answer:

prompt: Describe the different groups living in Ireland in 1500.

prompt: Describe how the Ulster Plantation was organised.

prompt: Describe a plantation town.

prompt: Say in your own words: how did the Ulster Plantation change Ulster?

prompt: Describe Cromwell's conquest and its results.

model_answer:
(i) My name is Cormac and I am a native Irishman from Co. Tyrone. I lost my land in the Plantation of Ulster, which began in 1609.
Our chief, Hugh O'Neill, led the Nine Years' War against Queen Elizabeth I, but he was defeated at the Battle of Kinsale in 1601. In 1607 O'Neill, O'Donnell and the other Ulster earls fled to Europe in the Flight of the Earls. King James I then took their land.
The land of six counties was taken: Armagh, Cavan, Coleraine, Donegal, Fermanagh and Tyrone. It was surveyed in 1609 and given out to new owners. Undertakers from England and Scotland got the best land and had to bring in British tenants. Servitors, soldiers from the war, also got land.
My family had farmed our land for generations under Brehon law, but now it was given to a Scottish undertaker. Some 'loyal Irish' were allowed to keep a little land, but they paid the highest rent. We were pushed onto poor, boggy land in the hills.
The settlers built strong houses with bawns, stone walls to protect them from people like us. New towns were built with a square called The Diamond, and Coleraine was given to London companies and renamed Londonderry.
The planters were Protestant and spoke English, and they brought English law. Our Catholic religion, our Irish language and our Brehon law were pushed aside.
I was angry at losing my land and my way of life. In 1641 many of us rose up in rebellion to try to win our land back.

prompt: Who was the British king when the American Revolution began?
explanation: King George III ruled Britain in 1775. By then relations with the colonists were very poor.

prompt: Which old idea did Enlightenment thinkers question?
options: The right to a fair trial
The idea that all men are equal
explanation: The divine right of kings was the belief that God chose kings to rule. Enlightenment thinkers questioned it.

prompt: Which American spent time in France and took up Enlightenment ideas?
explanation: Benjamin Franklin lived in France for a time and brought back these new ideas.

prompt: How did the French and Indian War help cause the revolution?
options: Britain kept 10,000 soldiers in America and made colonists pay for them
France took over the thirteen colonies and raised taxes
The colonists lost and had to give land to Spain
Britain banned colonists from joining its army
explanation: After the war Britain kept soldiers in America and taxed the colonists to pay for them, which made them angry.

prompt: What did the Navigation Acts say?
options: Colonists had to pay a tax on newspapers
Goods like tobacco and sugar could be sold only to Britain
Colonists had to house and feed British troops
Only British ships could fish off the American coast
explanation: The Navigation Acts said some American goods could be sold only to Britain, so merchants began smuggling.

prompt: Which 1765 law taxed documents like newspapers, playing cards and wills?
explanation: The Stamp Act of 1765 put a tax on printed papers and documents.

prompt: What did the Quartering Act (1765) force colonists to do?
explanation: Quartering means giving soldiers a place to stay. Colonists had to house and feed British troops.

prompt: What did the slogan 'no taxation without representation' mean?
options: Colonists refused to pay any taxes to their own assemblies
Colonists wanted lower taxes on goods from France
Colonists should not pay British taxes because they had no MPs in London
Only landowners should be allowed to vote in America
explanation: The colonists had no MPs in the British parliament, so they felt Britain had no right to tax them.

prompt: What happened at the Boston Massacre in 1770?
options: Washington crossed the icy Delaware River
Rebels dumped 342 chests of tea into the harbour
The Minutemen fought the British for the first time
British soldiers fired on a crowd and killed five men
explanation: At the Boston Massacre British soldiers shot into a crowd and killed five colonists.

prompt: What happened at the Boston Tea Party in 1773?
options: Delegates from the colonies met to plan a boycott
Rebels dressed as Mohawks dumped 342 chests of tea into Boston Harbour
British soldiers seized tea from American merchants
Colonists held a party to celebrate the end of the war
explanation: The Sons of Liberty, dressed as Mohawks, threw the tea into the harbour as a protest against British taxes.

prompt: How did Britain punish Boston after the Tea Party?
options: It banned all colonists from drinking tea
It gave the city to France
It passed the 'Intolerable Acts' and closed the port
It hanged the leaders of the Sons of Liberty
explanation: Britain passed the 'Intolerable Acts' (1774-1775), which closed the port of Boston.

prompt: Who were the Sons of Liberty?
options: British soldiers sent to keep order in Boston
Merchants who supported the Navigation Acts
French soldiers who helped the Americans
A semi-secret group who wanted Americans to govern themselves
explanation: The Sons of Liberty were a semi-secret group who wanted self-government for America.

prompt: What did the First Continental Congress (1774) call for?
explanation: Delegates from all thirteen colonies met in Philadelphia and called for a boycott, or refusal to buy, British goods.

prompt: Where were the first shots of the war fired in April 1775?
explanation: The Minutemen fought British troops at Lexington and Concord in April 1775. The war had begun.

prompt: Who were the Minutemen?
options: Spies who worked for King George III
Amateur soldiers ready to fight at a minute's notice
explanation: The Minutemen were a Boston militia, ready to fight at a minute's notice.

prompt: When was the Declaration of Independence approved?
explanation: The Second Continental Congress approved it on 4 July 1776. Americans still celebrate Independence Day on 4 July.

prompt: Who wrote most of the Declaration of Independence?
explanation: Thomas Jefferson was the main writer of the Declaration of Independence.

prompt: Why was the Battle of Saratoga (1777) a turning point?
options: France, then Spain and the Netherlands, joined the American side
The British navy was destroyed there
It was the first battle of the war
explanation: The American win at Saratoga persuaded France, then Spain and the Netherlands, to help the Americans.

prompt: What happened at Trenton in 1776?
options: The British won but lost more men
Rebels dumped tea into the river
Cornwallis surrendered to a French and American force
Washington crossed the icy Delaware River and made a surprise attack
explanation: Washington crossed the frozen Delaware River and surprised the enemy. This was guerrilla warfare.

prompt: Which battle in 1781 decided the war?
explanation: At Yorktown, Washington and a French fleet trapped Cornwallis, who surrendered.

prompt: What is guerrilla warfare?
options: Two big armies meeting on an open battlefield
Surprise ambushes and hit-and-run attacks against a bigger enemy
Fighting a battle at sea with a large navy
Starving a town until it surrenders
explanation: Guerrilla warfare uses surprise and quick attacks, which suits a smaller force.

prompt: What did Baron von Steuben do at Valley Forge?
options: Led the French fleet at Yorktown
Trained the soldiers in drills, tactics and discipline
explanation: Von Steuben trained Washington's army during the hard winter of 1777-78, making it much better.

prompt: Which of these helped the Americans win?
options: Britain had no allies against them
They had the greatest navy in the world
They knew the countryside and the British were 3,000 miles from home
Their soldiers were full-time and highly disciplined
explanation: The Americans had home advantage, while the British had to send soldiers and supplies across the ocean.

prompt: Which treaty ended the war in 1783?
explanation: In the Treaty of Paris (1783) Britain recognised the United States of America.

prompt: Who did NOT get rights such as the vote under the new American system?
options: Soldiers who fought in the war
explanation: The Bill of Rights gave rights like free speech, but women could not vote and slaves were not free.

prompt: How did the American Revolution affect France?
options: It had to pay Britain huge sums for losing the war
It nearly went bankrupt, which helped cause its own revolution
It became a republic straight away in 1783
It gained the thirteen colonies from Britain in 1783
explanation: Helping the Americans cost France so much that new taxes were needed. This helped cause the French Revolution in 1789.

prompt: Which Irish leader was inspired by the American Revolution?
explanation: Wolfe Tone and the United Irishmen were inspired by America. This led to the 1798 Rebellion.

prompt: Who became the first president of the USA in 1789?
explanation: George Washington, who led the Continental Army, became the first president in 1789.

prompt: Say in your own words: what is a revolution?
model_answer: A revolution is when people overthrow their rulers. They then set up a new system of government. The American colonists did this when they broke away from Britain.

prompt: Say in your own words: why were the colonists angry about British taxes?
model_answer: Britain had a big debt after the French and Indian War, so it added taxes like the Stamp Act and Townshend Acts. The colonists had no MPs in London to speak for them. Their slogan was "no taxation without representation".

prompt: Describe the Boston Tea Party and what Britain did next.
model_answer: In 1773 the Sons of Liberty, dressed as Mohawks, dumped 342 chests of tea into Boston Harbour. Britain punished Boston with the "Intolerable Acts" and closed the port.

prompt: Explain how the war began in 1775.
model_answer: In 1774 the First Continental Congress called for a boycott of British goods. In April 1775 the Minutemen fought British troops at Lexington and Concord. Paul Revere rode ahead to warn that the British were coming.

prompt: Say in your own words: what was the Declaration of Independence?
model_answer: It was the document approved on 4 July 1776 that declared America free of British rule. Thomas Jefferson wrote most of it. It said all men are created equal, with rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.

prompt: Explain why Saratoga and Yorktown were important battles.
model_answer: Saratoga (1777) was an American win and the turning point, because France, then Spain and the Netherlands, joined the Americans. At Yorktown (1781) Washington and a French fleet trapped Cornwallis, who surrendered. This decided the war.

prompt: Give three reasons why the Americans beat the British.
model_answer: The Americans knew the countryside, while the British were 3,000 miles from home. Baron von Steuben trained the army at Valley Forge. France, Spain and the Netherlands gave money, ships and soldiers.

prompt: Describe three results of the American Revolution.
model_answer: The USA became independent after the Treaty of Paris in 1783. The Constitution (1787) set up an elected government, and Washington became the first president in 1789. France nearly went bankrupt helping America, which helped cause the French Revolution, and Wolfe Tone in Ireland was inspired.

(b) Causes: Britain had a huge debt after the French and Indian War, so it kept 10,000 soldiers in America and made the colonists pay for them. prompt:
People in History. Select one of the people described below. Write about that person.
(i) A named revolutionary leader (in America or France or Ireland) during the Age of Revolutions, 1770-1815.
HINTS: Early life; Ideas; Main events of the revolution; Results of the revolution.
model_answer:
My name is George Washington, leader of the Continental Army in the American Revolution.
Early life: As a young man I fought for Britain in the French and Indian War against the French and their Native American allies. This gave me military experience.
Ideas: Like many colonists I was angry about British taxes such as the Stamp Act, because we had no MPs in London: "no taxation without representation". We wanted to stop being ruled by a king and set up a republic.
Main events: In 1775 the Second Continental Congress made me commander-in-chief. On 4 July 1776 Congress approved the Declaration of Independence, written mainly by Thomas Jefferson. In December 1776 I led my men across the icy Delaware River for a surprise attack at Trenton. In the winter of 1777-78 we camped at Valley Forge, where over 2,000 of my men died of cold, hunger and disease, but Baron von Steuben trained us in drills and discipline. After our win at Saratoga, France joined us. In 1781 I trapped Cornwallis at Yorktown with the help of a French fleet, and he surrendered.
Results: The Treaty of Paris (1783) recognised the United States. The Constitution (1787) set up an elected government, and in 1789 I became the first president of the USA. Our revolution also helped cause the French Revolution and inspired Wolfe Tone in Ireland.
marking_scheme: Marked on the SRS (Significant Relevant Statement) system. Full SRS = 4 marks; content max 20 marks (5 SRS). Overall mark (quality of the whole answer) max 5 marks. The leader must be named; if no leader is named, award relevant material and max 2 on the overall mark. Examples: America - Washington; France - Robespierre; Ireland - Wolfe Tone. Any aspect of the leader's life is accepted: background, course of the revolution, results. Background material = one SRS only.

prompt: Who organised the 1798 Rebellion?
explanation: The Society of United Irishmen, a secret republican society, organised the rising.

prompt: Where and when was the Society of United Irishmen founded?
explanation: The society was founded in Belfast in October 1791. Tone then set up a Dublin branch.

prompt: What was the motto of the United Irishmen?
options: Liberty, equality and fraternity for all
For God, for Ulster and for the King
To unite Catholic, Protestant and Dissenter as Irishmen
explanation: They wanted all religions to unite as Irish people with equal rights.

prompt: What was the newspaper of the United Irishmen called?
explanation: The Northern Star spread their ideas. At first they used peaceful means.

prompt: What is a republic?
options: A country whose people elect their leaders, with an elected president instead of a king
A colony ruled by a governor from another country
A country ruled by a king chosen by God
A country run by the leaders of one church
explanation: In a republic the head of state is an elected president, not a king or queen.

prompt: What does 'secular' mean?
options: Not run according to religious beliefs
Ruled by a king or queen
explanation: The United Irishmen wanted a secular republic, not run by any religion.

prompt: Which revolution had the motto "liberty, equality and fraternity"?
explanation: The French Revolution (1789) overthrew the king. Its ideas spread in Ireland, especially among Presbyterians in Belfast.

prompt: In the 1700s, the Anglicans were 15 per cent of the people. How much of the land did they own?
explanation: The Protestant Ascendancy owned 80 per cent of the land, much of it taken from Catholics in the plantations.

prompt: What were the Penal Laws?
options: Laws that sent prisoners to Australia
Laws that gave Catholics equal rights
Laws that taxed tea, paper and sugar
explanation: The Penal Laws, from the 1690s, treated Catholics (and less so Presbyterians) unfairly.

prompt: What is Catholic emancipation?
options: Letting Catholics leave Ireland for France
Giving Catholics equal rights, especially the right to sit in parliament
explanation: Henry Grattan wanted Catholic emancipation, but Britain blocked it.

prompt: Who were the Dissenters?
options: Catholics who refused to pay rent
Soldiers who left the British army
Protestants, such as Presbyterians, who were not part of the Anglican Church
explanation: Dissenters were Protestants outside the Anglican Church. Most were Presbyterians in Ulster.

prompt: What happened at Bantry Bay in December 1796?
options: A storm forced a French fleet of 43 ships to turn back
The rebels won their first battle
explanation: France sent 43 ships and 14,000 soldiers, but a storm off Bantry Bay forced them home.

prompt: Who were the Yeomanry?
options: French soldiers who landed at Killala
Local part-time soldiers loyal to the government
Members of the Catholic Defenders group
Rebels who fought in County Wexford
explanation: The Yeomanry were local part-time soldiers. They burned houses and tortured suspects.

prompt: What was pitch-capping?
options: A way of signalling to French ships
A secret oath of the United Irishmen
A tax paid on hats and caps
A torture using a cap of hot tar on the head
explanation: Pitch-capping was one of the cruel tortures used against suspected rebels in 1797-98.

prompt: Which Catholic group did the United Irishmen join with?
explanation: After they were banned, the United Irishmen collected arms and joined with the Defenders.

prompt: Which county saw the most intense fighting in 1798?
explanation: Wexford saw the most intense rebel activity, led by Fr John Murphy and Bagenal Harvey.

prompt: Where were the Wexford rebels crushed on 21 June 1798?
explanation: General Lake's 13,000 troops, with cannon, defeated the rebels at Vinegar Hill.

prompt: Which Wexford priest led rebels in 1798?
explanation: Fr John Murphy and Bagenal Harvey led the rebels in Wexford.

prompt: What happened at Scullabogue?
options: The rising began with attacks on mail coaches
explanation: At Scullabogue and Wexford Bridge rebels killed mostly Protestant prisoners. This was sectarian violence.

prompt: Who led the rebels in Ulster?
options: Fr John Murphy and Bagenal Harvey
Henry Joy McCracken and Henry Munro
explanation: Most Ulster rebels were Presbyterians. They lost at Antrim and Ballynahinch.

prompt: Where did General Humbert land in August 1798?
explanation: Humbert landed at Killala with over 1,000 French soldiers.

prompt: What were 'the Races of Castlebar'?
options: A horse race held to raise money for the rebels
A march of Yeomanry through Mayo
The final defeat of the French
A French and rebel victory in Co. Mayo
explanation: Humbert's French soldiers and the rebels won at Castlebar. They then lost at Ballinamuck, Co. Longford.

prompt: Which of these is a reason the rebellion failed?
options: Informers gave the government the names of leaders
The French sent too many soldiers
The rebels had more cannons than the army
Britain had no army in Ireland
explanation: Informers, poor weapons, little training and late French help all caused the failure.

prompt: What did the Act of Union (1800) do?
options: It ended all the Penal Laws
It gave Ireland its own president
It gave Catholics the vote at last
explanation: From 1801 Irish MPs went to London. Ireland was ruled from there until 1922.

prompt: Who led a failed rising in Dublin in 1803?
explanation: Robert Emmet's 1803 rising failed and he was executed.

prompt: What is the 'physical force tradition'?
options: Refusing to pay rent to landlords
Training soldiers for the British army
Using peaceful votes in parliament to win change
Using violent rebellion to try to win Irish independence
explanation: Tone's rebellion inspired later risings in 1848, 1867 and 1916.

prompt: About how many people died in the 1798 Rebellion?
explanation: Over 30,000 people died. Thousands of rebels were exiled or sent to prison in Australia.

prompt: Say in your own words: how did the Age of Revolution help cause the 1798 Rebellion?
model_answer: The American Revolution showed that Britain could be beaten. The French Revolution overthrew a king and set up a republic with the motto "liberty, equality and fraternity". These ideas spread in Ireland, especially among Presbyterians in Belfast.

prompt: Explain how land and the Penal Laws made people angry in the 1700s.
model_answer: The Anglican Protestant Ascendancy were 15 per cent of the people but owned 80 per cent of the land, and rents were high. The Penal Laws discriminated against Catholics and, less so, Presbyterians. Only Anglicans could sit in parliament.

prompt: Describe the aims of the United Irishmen.
model_answer: They wanted to unite Catholic, Protestant and Dissenter as Irishmen with equal rights, including Catholic emancipation. They wanted less British interference and later an independent secular republic.

prompt: Explain why the United Irishmen changed from peaceful to armed methods.
model_answer: Britain went to war with France in 1793, and in 1794 a French agent was caught with papers naming Tone. The United Irishmen were banned. They became a secret society, collected arms and joined with the Defenders.

prompt: Describe the government reign of terror of 1797-98.
model_answer: The Insurrection Act allowed martial law. Soldiers and the Yeomanry burned houses and tortured suspects with pitch-capping and half-hanging. Informers helped arrest leaders like Lord Edward Fitzgerald.

prompt: Describe what happened in Wexford in 1798.
model_answer: Wexford saw the most intense fighting, led by Fr John Murphy. Rebels won at Oulart Hill and took Enniscorthy and Wexford town, but lost at New Ross and Arklow. On 21 June General Lake crushed them at Vinegar Hill.

prompt: Give four reasons why the 1798 Rebellion failed.
model_answer: Informers gave away the leaders. The rebels were amateur soldiers with little training. They had pikes and a few muskets against cannons. French help came too late and with too few soldiers.

prompt: Describe three results of the 1798 Rebellion.
model_answer: Over 30,000 people died. The Act of Union (1800) abolished the Irish parliament, so Ireland was ruled from London. Tone became the "father of Irish republicanism" and inspired the physical force tradition, while the massacres made many Protestants support the union.

prompt:
This question is on pre-twentieth century revolutions/rebellions.
(a) Name a revolution you studied from pre-twentieth century Europe or the wider world.
(b) Write an account of the causes and/or consequences of the revolution you studied.
model_answer:
(a) The 1798 Rebellion in Ireland.
(b) Causes: The American Revolution showed Britain could be beaten, and the French Revolution (1789) spread ideas of "liberty, equality and fraternity", especially among Presbyterians in Belfast. The Anglican Protestant Ascendancy were 15 per cent of the people but owned 80 per cent of the land. The Penal Laws discriminated against Catholics and Presbyterians, and only Anglicans could sit in parliament. The United Irishmen, founded in Belfast in 1791 by Wolfe Tone and others, wanted equal rights for all. When they were banned in 1794 they turned to physical force. The government reign of terror in 1797 (pitch-capping, half-hanging, burning houses) pushed people to rise in May 1798.
Consequences: Over 30,000 people died and thousands were exiled or sent to Australia. The Act of Union (1800) abolished the Irish parliament, so from 1801 Ireland was ruled from London. Tone became the "father of Irish republicanism" and started the physical force tradition (1848, 1867, 1916). The massacres of Protestants at Scullabogue made many Protestants support the union, and the Orange Order grew.
marking_scheme:
(a) Name of a valid revolution/rebellion: 3 marks.
(b) 3 marks for each valid, relevant point explaining a cause or consequence, up to 18 marks. Two undeveloped points = 3 marks. A list of undeveloped points = 6 marks max. One incomplete concluding point = 2 marks max.

prompt:
People in History. Select one of the people described below. Write about that person.
(i) A named revolutionary leader (in America or France or Ireland) during the Age of Revolutions, 1770-1815.
HINTS: Early life; Ideas; Main events of the revolution; Results of the revolution.
model_answer:
My name is Theobald Wolfe Tone, a Protestant and a leader of the United Irishmen.
Ideas: I was inspired by the American and French Revolutions. In 1791 I wrote a pamphlet saying Protestants and Catholics should have equal rights. I wanted to unite Catholic, Protestant and Dissenter under the common name of Irishman and to set up a secular Irish republic, separate from Britain.
Main events: In October 1791 the Society of United Irishmen was founded in Belfast, and I set up a Dublin branch. At first we were peaceful, with our newspaper The Northern Star. In 1794 a French agent was caught with papers naming me, and we were banned, so we turned to physical force. I went to France for help. In December 1796 France sent 43 ships and 14,000 soldiers, but a storm at Bantry Bay forced them home. The rising began on 23 May 1798. The worst fighting was in Wexford, where the rebels were crushed at Vinegar Hill. In August General Humbert landed at Killala and won at Castlebar but lost at Ballinamuck. In October a French fleet was beaten off Donegal. I was arrested and took my own life.
Results: Over 30,000 people died. The Act of Union (1800) abolished the Irish parliament. But I became the "father of Irish republicanism", and my ideas inspired later risings in 1848, 1867 and 1916.
marking_scheme: Marked on the SRS (Significant Relevant Statement) system. Full SRS = 4 marks; content max 20 marks (5 SRS). Overall mark (quality of the whole answer) max 5 marks. The leader must be named; if no leader is named, award relevant material and max 2 on the overall mark. Examples: America - Washington; France - Robespierre; Ireland - Wolfe Tone. Any aspect of the leader's life is accepted: background, course of the revolution, results. Background material = one SRS only.

prompt:
Based on your study of the 1798 Rebellion:
(a) Explain the term 'physical force tradition'.
(b) Name one leader of the rebellion.
(c) Mention two reasons why the rebellion failed.
(d) Write an account of the results of the rebellion.
model_answer:
(a) Using violent rebellion (armed force) to try to win Irish independence, as the United Irishmen did in 1798.
(b) Wolfe Tone (also: Fr John Murphy, Henry Joy McCracken, Lord Edward Fitzgerald).
(c) 1. Informers gave the government the names of the leaders. 2. French help came too late and with too few soldiers.
(d) Over 30,000 people died and thousands of rebels were exiled or sent to prison in Australia. The Act of Union (1800) abolished the Irish parliament, so from 1801 Ireland was ruled from London. Robert Emmet led a failed rising in 1803. Tone became the "father of Irish republicanism", inspiring later risings in 1848, 1867 and 1916. The massacres made many Protestants support the union, and the Orange Order grew.
marking_scheme:
(a) Clear explanation: 3 marks (vague = 1-2 marks).
(b) Any valid leader: 3 marks.
(c) Two valid reasons, 3 marks each (6 marks): informers / amateur soldiers / poor weapons / French help too late or too small.
(d) 3 marks per valid result or development, 6 marks max here (e.g. deaths, Act of Union, Emmet 1803, physical force tradition, Protestants back the union).

prompt: When did the Great Famine happen?
explanation: The Great Famine, An Gorta Mór, lasted from 1845 to 1850.

prompt: What is blight?
options: A fungus that rots potatoes in the ground
explanation: Blight is a fungal disease spread by spores in the air. It makes potatoes rot and become inedible.

prompt: Where was blight seen in Europe in June 1845, before it reached Ireland?
explanation: Blight came from the USA to Belgium in June 1845, then spread to Ireland by August 1845.

prompt: When did blight reach Ireland?
explanation: Blight reached Ireland in August 1845 and destroyed one-third of the crop that year.

prompt: What was an absentee landlord?
options: A tenant who left the country without paying
A landlord who refused to collect rent
A landlord who did not live on the estate and left an agent to run it
A landlord who lived in a one-roomed cabin
explanation: About half of the 20,000 landlords lived away, in Dublin or England.

prompt: What was conacre?
options: One acre of land given in return for work
A tax paid to the landlord every year
A type of potato grown in the west
A government food depot in a town
explanation: Cottiers worked for a farmer in return for one acre of land. This was called conacre.

prompt: What is subsistence farming?
options: Growing just enough to eat and pay the rent
explanation: Many Irish families grew just enough to survive, with almost nothing left over.

prompt: What was subdivision?
options: Dividing a farm between all the sons, so farms got smaller
Joining small farms into big ones
Splitting a farm into crops and pasture
explanation: With subdivision, farms got smaller and smaller with each generation.

prompt: What happened to Ireland's population between 1790 and 1840?
options: It doubled from four million to eight million
It stayed at about six million
It grew from one million to two million
It halved from eight million to four million
explanation: People married young and had large families, and smallpox vaccination lowered the death rate.

prompt: Why did so many Irish people rely on the potato?
options: Potatoes could be stored for many years
Potatoes were imported cheaply from America
One acre could feed six people for ten months
explanation: Potatoes grew well in Ireland and fed a lot of people from a small amount of land.

prompt: What was the Lumper?
options: The type of potato that made up 90 per cent of the crop
explanation: The Lumper was the main potato grown, so blight hit almost the whole crop.

prompt: What is monoculture?
options: Growing only one crop, such as potatoes
explanation: Depending on one crop made Ireland very vulnerable when blight struck.

prompt: Why is 1847 called 'Black '47'?
options: The Famine was at its worst because few seeds had been planted
Blight destroyed every potato in Europe
explanation: In 1847 the crop did not fail, but so few potatoes had been planted that the Famine was at its worst.

prompt: What caused most deaths in the Famine ('famine fever')?
options: Diseases such as typhus, dysentery and cholera
explanation: Most people died of disease, which spread among weak, hungry people.

prompt: What is eviction?
options: Paying the rent late to a landlord
Moving to a new farm by choice
Forcing a tenant out of their home
explanation: About 500,000 people were evicted. Landlords took the roofs off houses so people could not return.

prompt: What did the government refuse to do about grain during the Famine?
explanation: Grain was still exported (284,000 tons in 1846), and troops protected the grain trade.

prompt: What was 'Peel's brimstone'?
options: A tax on potatoes sold at market
Hard, yellow Indian corn from America
explanation: Peel imported Indian corn (maize). Many people did not know how to cook it.

prompt: What did the Public Works Act (1846) give people?
options: Paid work building famine roads and piers
explanation: People earned a small wage on public works, but the work was exhausting for hungry people.

prompt: What is laissez-faire?
options: The government interfering as little as possible
A French name for a soup kitchen
The government controlling all food prices
A law that banned all emigration
explanation: Lord John Russell followed laissez-faire, so the government did not do enough to help.

prompt: Who was in charge of famine relief under Lord John Russell?
explanation: Charles Trevelyan cut back the public works.

prompt: Why was the workhouse a last resort?
options: It was always in another country
Families were split up and disease spread there
It cost a lot of money to get in
explanation: Workhouses gave food and shelter for work, but families were kept apart and disease spread.

prompt: Which religious group opened soup kitchens and raised about £200,000?
explanation: The Quakers (Society of Friends) were famous for their famine relief.

prompt: Which Native American nation sent $170 to help Irish famine victims?
explanation: The Choctaw Nation gave $170, a huge sum for them.

prompt: About how many people died in the Great Famine?
explanation: About one million died, and about one and a half million emigrated.

prompt: What was a coffin ship?
options: A ship that carried food to Ireland
A warship used in the war with France
A ship that carried coffins for burials
A famine-era emigrant ship on which many passengers died
explanation: Crowded, dirty emigrant ships were called coffin ships because so many people died on them.

prompt: How did the Famine affect the Irish language?
options: It declined faster, as Irish-speaking areas lost most people
It spread to Britain and America
It became the main language of Dublin
It was banned by law in 1847
explanation: The west, where most Irish speakers lived, was worst hit by death and emigration.

prompt: What is the Irish Diaspora?
options: The Irish people who stayed in Ireland after the Famine
All the Irish people and their descendants who live outside Ireland
A group that helped famine victims
explanation: The Irish Diaspora numbers about seventy million people today.

prompt: Where did many Irish emigrants die in quarantine in 1847?
explanation: About 100,000 Irish arrived in Canada in 1847. Many died in quarantine at Grosse Ile.

prompt: Say in your own words: why did the potato blight cause a famine in Ireland but not elsewhere?
model_answer: Most poor Irish people lived on potatoes and little else, especially the Lumper. Other countries had other foods to eat. When blight rotted the potatoes, Ireland's rural poor had nothing to fall back on.

prompt: Explain how population growth and subdivision made Ireland vulnerable.
model_answer: The population doubled from four million in 1790 to eight million in 1840. Farmers divided their land between their sons, so farms got very small. These tiny farms could only grow enough potatoes to survive.

prompt: Describe the four main groups in rural Ireland before the Famine.
model_answer: Landlords owned almost all the land, and about half were absentee. Tenant farmers rented land. Cottiers worked for a farmer in return for one acre (conacre), and landless labourers lived in one-roomed cabins and took work where they could.

prompt: Describe what happened in the Famine year by year from 1845 to 1850.
model_answer: In 1845 blight destroyed one-third of the crop, and in 1846 three-quarters. Black '47 was the worst year because few potatoes had been planted. Blight returned in 1848, and by 1850 the crop had recovered.

prompt: Describe Peel's relief scheme.
model_answer: In 1845 Sir Robert Peel set up a Relief Commission with 600 food depots. He imported Indian corn, called "Peel's brimstone". The Public Works Act (1846) gave paid work building roads and piers.

prompt: Explain how laissez-faire affected relief under Lord John Russell.
model_answer: Russell believed the government should interfere as little as possible. Charles Trevelyan cut back the public works, and the soup kitchens ended after six months. Grain was still exported while people starved.

prompt: Give four consequences of the Great Famine.
model_answer: About one million people died and 1.5 million emigrated, many on coffin ships. The Irish language declined faster. Subdivision stopped, and anger at Britain grew.

prompt: Describe the Irish Diaspora in one country.
model_answer: In the USA the Irish started at the bottom and faced discrimination, but rose up. Today 40 million Americans have Irish roots. Famous Irish Americans include John F. Kennedy and Joe Biden.

prompt:
Over one million people emigrated from Ireland in the 1840s/1850s. The following sources relate to a ship containing Irish emigrants which arrived in New York on 30 November 1853. Examine the sources and answer the questions which follow.
Source 1: extract from a newspaper report describing the ship and its passengers.
The ship, Marathon, left Liverpool on the 22nd of September, with 522 passengers, mostly Irish. She arrived at New York after a voyage of 59 days, during which she lost 64 persons to an outbreak of cholera.
The passengers were in a state of the most wretched poverty and filth. They were lodged on two decks, one above the other. The decks were covered with reeking filth.
The passengers' provisions [food supplies] were exhausted three weeks before the ship came into port. Had the ship been delayed for a few days longer, the people would have starved.
(a) From where did the Marathon set sail and how long did the journey take?
(b) How many of the passengers survived, and how many died, on the voyage to New York?
(c) In Source 1, what were three difficulties faced by passengers on the Marathon? Support each point with reference to the source.
model_answer:
(a) It set sail from Liverpool. The journey took 59 days.
(b) Survived: 458 (522 - 64). Died: 64.
(c) 1. Disease: 64 people died "to an outbreak of cholera".
2. Dirt and poverty: the passengers were in "wretched poverty and filth" and the decks were "covered with reeking filth".
3. Hunger: their food supplies "were exhausted three weeks before the ship came into port", so they nearly starved. (Also: the long 59-day voyage.)
marking_scheme:
(a) Liverpool 3 marks + 59 days 3 marks (6).
(b) Survived = 458 (3 marks); Died = 64 (3 marks) (6).
(c) Three points with evidence from the source, each on a sliding scale of 3 (3 = very good, 2 = fair/good, 1 = weak) (9). Could refer to the length of the voyage / cholera or sickness / lack of hygiene / shortage of food or starvation.

Document 1: an extract about life during the Famine in Ireland (from 'Light and Shades of Ireland' by Asenath Nicholson, London, 1850).

He demanded of her to show him the potatoes - she hesitated; he asked her what she had in the pot - she was silent: he looked in and saw a dog with the handful of potatoes that she had gathered from the field.
The sight of the wretched cabin, and still more, the despairing looks of the poor silent mother and the famished children, crouched in fear in a dark corner, so touched the magistrate that he took the pot from the fire, instructed the woman to follow him and they went to the courtroom together.
He presented the pot, containing the dog and the handful of potatoes, to the astonished Judge. She told him that they sat in their desolate (wretched) cabin two entire days, without eating, before she killed the half-famished (starved) dog. The Judge gave her three pence from his own purse and told her when she had used that to come again to him.'

(iv) Yes. He was so touched by the starving mother and children that he took the pot from the fire and went with her to the courtroom to show the judge how bad things were.
(v) The Judge was astonished. He gave her three pence from his own purse and told her to come back to him when it was used up.

prompt:
Based on your study of the Great Famine:
(a) Explain two causes of the Great Famine apart from potato blight.
(b) What efforts were made by the British government to provide relief to the starving Irish?
(c) Explain the significance of the Irish Diaspora, with reference to one country.
model_answer:
(a) 1. Reliance on the potato: most poor people lived on potatoes alone (in Mayo nine out of ten people), so when the crop failed they had no other food.
2. Population growth and subdivision: the population doubled to eight million by 1840, and farms were divided between sons until they were tiny.
(b) Peel set up a Relief Commission with 600 food depots in 1845 and imported Indian corn ("Peel's brimstone"). The Public Works Act (1846) gave paid work building roads and piers. Under Russell, the Soup Kitchen Act (1847) gave free soup for six months, and workhouses gave food and shelter in return for work. But laissez-faire meant help was limited and grain exports were not banned.
(c) USA: Irish emigrants started at the bottom and faced discrimination, but rose up over time. Today 40 million Americans have Irish roots Famous Irish Americans include John F. Kennedy and Joe Biden. The Diaspora of about seventy million people keeps strong links between Ireland and the world.
marking_scheme:

(b) 3 marks per valid relief measure or development, max 9: Relief Commission / Indian corn / public works / soup kitchens / workhouses (credit comments on laissez-faire).
(c) Country named and significance explained: 6 marks (3 per developed point).

My name is Michael Collins.
I took part in the 1916 Rising. After the surrender I was one of about 3,000 people arrested and sent to camps like Frongoch. When I was released I joined Sinn Féin, which won 73 of 105 seats in the 1918 election and set up the First Dáil in January 1919.

prompt:
The introduction of the Third Home Rule Bill in the House of Commons led to the "Home Rule Crisis", 1912-1914. Study the source below and answer the questions which follow.
Source 1: Extracts from speeches by party leaders in the House of Commons, 11 April 1912.
[Picture: photographs of H. H. Asquith, Edward Carson and John Redmond, each beside his speech]
H. H. Asquith: 'This Bill will give to the Irish people an opportunity for the development of their own national life. At the same time, it will bind them to us and the Empire by a sense of voluntary cooperation and loyal attachment.'
Edward Carson: 'The proposals that we have heard here today are absolutely unworkable and ridiculous. My party has a duty to oppose this Bill with all the energy we can. We believe it to be a fatal Bill for our country.'
John Redmond: 'This is a great historical occasion. I thank God that I have lived to see this day. I believe this Bill will turn Ireland into a happy and prosperous country, with a united, loyal, and contented people.'
(a) Fill in the names of the leaders in the box below.
Name of leader | Role in parliament
 | Leader of the Unionist Party
 | Leader of the Home Rule Party (Irish Parliamentary Party)
 | Prime Minister and leader of the Liberal Party
(b) Insert a tick for each party leader to indicate whether he was for or against Home Rule. (H. H. Asquith / Edward Carson / John Redmond: For Home Rule OR Against Home Rule)
(c) Using Source 1, explain how you know that each leader was either for or against Home Rule. (H. H. Asquith / Edward Carson / John Redmond)
(d) Write an account of a leader who was involved in the parliamentary tradition in Irish politics. Your account could include points such as: when and why the leader became involved in politics; political events/campaigns in which the leader took part; the leader's role in parliament; success and/or failure in the leader's political career, etc. Name of leader:
model_answer:
(a) Leader of the Unionist Party: Edward Carson. Leader of the Home Rule Party: John Redmond. Prime Minister and leader of the Liberal Party: H. H. Asquith.
(b) Asquith: for. Carson: against. Redmond: for.
(c) Asquith: he says the Bill will give the Irish people "an opportunity for the development of their own national life", so he supports it.
Carson: he calls the proposals "absolutely unworkable and ridiculous" and says his party will "oppose this Bill with all the energy we can", so he is against it.
Redmond: he thanks God he has "lived to see this day" and believes the Bill will make Ireland "happy and prosperous", so he is for it.
(d) Name of leader: John Redmond.
Redmond led the Home Rule Party (Irish Parliamentary Party). He wanted Home Rule, a parliament in Dublin for Irish affairs, won by peaceful means in parliament: the parliamentary tradition.
After the 1910 elections the Liberal leader Herbert Asquith needed Redmond's votes to stay in power, so Redmond demanded Home Rule in return.
The Parliament Act (1911) stopped the House of Lords from blocking it, so the Third Home Rule Bill (1912) was due to become law in 1914.
Unionists led by Carson fought it with the Covenant and the UVF, and nationalists set up the Irish Volunteers.
His success: Home Rule became law in September 1914. But it was delayed until after World War One.
Redmond told the Irish Volunteers to join the British army. Most did, but the movement split.
After the 1916 Rising and the executions, support swung to Sinn Féin. In the 1918 election his party won only 6 seats, while Sinn Féin won 73, so his career ended in failure.
