The battle of the Four Courts marked the beginning of the Irish Civil War. In the grounds of the Four Courts, the Public Record Office (PRO) contained state records going back to the 1100s.

(a) Look at the photographs and match each one to the correct caption.
Caption | Photograph
Staff at work in the Public Record Office (PRO) in 1914. |
A huge explosion and fire destroy the PRO, 30 June 1922. |
Fragments of documents outside the GPO, a kilometre away. |

Archivist Catriona Crowe gave a talk on the destruction of the Public Record Office. Read this extract and answer the questions which follow.
In April 1922, an armed force of anti-Treaty IRA occupied the Four Courts. The government assault on the Four Courts began on 28 June. At 12.30 on 30 June, there was an enormous explosion, and fire spread to the Public Record Office.
Among the records lost in the fire were the census records of 1821, 1831, 1841 and 1851. Other records included church records dating back to 1174, court records, military records, and records dealing with the huge land transfers of the 17th century. It was one of the greatest cultural disasters ever to befall any country, and we did it to ourselves. What damage was done to writing Irish history based on primary sources we will never know.

(d) Opinion: "It was one of the greatest cultural disasters ever to befall any country." I agree, because records going back to the 1100s were lost for ever, so historians can never use those primary sources to write Irish history.
(e) 1. An archive keeps original documents, but a library has published books. 2. You must read archive documents in the archive, but you can borrow library books and take them home.
(f) The Civil War came from the split over the Anglo-Irish Treaty (1921). The pro-Treaty side, led by Griffith and Collins, said it was a stepping stone to a republic; the anti-Treaty side, led by de Valera, said it was not the republic people fought for. The Dáil accepted it by 64 votes to 57.

The war ended on 24 May 1923.
Its legacy was bitterness and two big parties, Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael, which came from the two sides.

prompt: Say in your own words: what is communism?
model_answer: Communism is based on the ideas of Karl Marx. The community owns all property, and people work for the good of the community and get what they need. In a communist state, the state controls all property.

prompt: Explain why there were two revolutions in Russia in 1917.
model_answer: World War One brought defeats and food shortages, and people blamed Tsar Nicholas II. In February protests over bread led him to abdicate, but the Provisional Government kept Russia in the war. In October Lenin's Bolsheviks, promising "Peace, Land, Bread!", took the Winter Palace.

prompt: Describe how Lenin set up a dictatorship.
model_answer: He abolished the Duma (parliament), and the Cheka secret police removed opponents. The tsar and his family were executed. Businesses were taken over by the state and land was taken from nobles and the Church.

prompt: Compare War Communism and the New Economic Policy.
model_answer: War Communism took food from peasants by force to feed soldiers and workers, which led to resistance and famine. The NEP (1921) let small businesses be private and peasants sell spare crops. It was mostly a success.

prompt: Describe how Stalin used terror.
model_answer: The NKVD killed his opponents or sent them to gulags. In the Great Purge senior communists faced show trials and "confessed". About one million people were put to death and another million sent to gulags.

prompt: Explain how Stalin used propaganda.
model_answer: Radio, posters, films and the newspaper Pravda praised him and attacked his enemies. Cities like Stalingrad were named after him and statues were put up everywhere. This built a cult of personality.

prompt: Describe collectivisation and its results.
model_answer: The state took over farmland and joined it into collective farms, and grain was requisitioned. Kulaks resisted and were shot or sent to gulags. A famine in 1932-1934 killed up to eight million, about four million in Ukraine.

prompt: Describe the Five-Year Plans.
model_answer: They aimed to make the USSR a modern industrial power fast. The first focused on coal, steel and electricity, and the third on weapons. Thirty million people moved to cities, and by 1940 only the USA made more.

## Document 2: de Gaulle's 'The Flame of French Resistance' speech, London, 18 June 1940 (edited English translation)
The leaders who, for many years past, have been at the head of the French armed forces have set up a government.
Alleging the defeat of our armies, this government has entered into negotiations with the enemy with a view to bringing about a cessation of hostilities.
It is quite true that we were, and still are, overwhelmed by enemy mechanised forces, both on the ground and in the air. It was the tanks, the planes, and the tactics of the Germans, far more than the fact that we were outnumbered, that forced our armies to retreat. It was the German tanks, planes, and tactics that provided the element of surprise which brought our leaders to their present plight.
But has the last word been said? Must we abandon all hope? Is our defeat final and irremediable? To those questions I answer - No!
For, remember this, France does not stand alone. She is not isolated. Behind her is a vast empire, and she can make common cause with the British empire, which commands the seas and is continuing the struggle. Like England, she can draw unreservedly on the immense industrial resources of the United States.
I, General de Gaulle, now in London, call on all French officers and men who are at present on British soil, or may be in the future, with or without their arms. I call on all engineers and skilled workmen from the armaments factories who are at present on British soil, or may be in the future, to get in touch with me.
Whatever happens, the flame of French resistance must not and shall not die.

prompt:
Tomi Reichental was born in Slovakia in 1935. He came to live in Ireland in 1959. In his autobiography, I Was a Boy in Belsen, he describes how his family was transported to the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp in 1944. Read the extract below and answer the questions which follow.
[Picture: photograph of Tomi Reichental as an old man, and the cover of his book I Was a Boy in Belsen]
"It was a box on wheels, the cattle carriage that we were in along with up to fifty others. There was straw on the floor and a large barrel in the centre, along with a couple of buckets. This was our toilet.
It was impossible to move, we were so tightly packed in together. The closing of the door behind us signified the end of our civilised life. We were no longer citizens, no longer human beings.
We were in that carriage for seven days. The train stopped on the evening of the 9th November. The doors were flung open. German voices began to scream at us, all at the same time, over and over again: 'HERAUS! HERAUS! SCHNELL! SCHNELL!' (OUT! OUT! HURRY! HURRY!)
There was a relentless barking that just wouldn't stop. Bright light flooded the carriage. Desperately frightened, I grabbed my mother's hand as everyone moved towards the entrance."
(a) What age was Tomi Reichental when he was transported to Bergen-Belsen in 1944?
(b) What hardships did the Reichental family endure on their way to Bergen-Belsen?
(c) What frightened Tomi Reichental when the train stopped?
(d) I was a Boy in Belsen by Tomi Reichental is an autobiography. What is the difference between a biography and an autobiography?
(e) Towards the end of his book Tomi Reichental writes that as one of the last Holocaust survivors he has a 'moral duty' to tell his story. Suggest two reasons why it is important that his story should be told.
(f) What is meant by the term, 'the Holocaust'?
(g) Apart from Jewish people in Europe, name two other groups of people who were targeted for persecution by the Nazis and explain why the Nazis persecuted them.
model_answer:
(a) He was 8 or 9 years old (born 1935, transported 1944).
(b) The family was packed into a cattle carriage, a "box on wheels", with up to fifty others, so tightly that nobody could move. A barrel and a couple of buckets were the only toilet. The journey lasted seven days, and they were no longer treated as citizens or human beings.
(c) German voices screamed at them over and over, "Out! Hurry!". There was relentless barking of dogs that would not stop, and a bright light suddenly flooded the carriage.
(d) A biography is the story of a person's life written by someone else. An autobiography is the story of a person's life written by that person.
(e) First, he is a survivor and an eyewitness, a primary source, and soon there will be no survivors left to tell what happened. Second, his story helps us remember the people who died and gives proof against people who deny the Holocaust happened.
(f) The Holocaust was the organised murder of six million Jewish people by the Nazis during World War Two.
(g) First group: Roma people (Gypsies). The Nazis saw them as an inferior race who did not belong in Germany, so they were sent to camps and murdered.
Second group: disabled people. The Nazis believed they weakened the "master race" and were a burden on the state, so many were killed.
(Other accepted groups: gay people, Jehovah's Witnesses, political enemies such as communists, pacifists, Slavic people.)

(b) Two points x 3 marks: cattle carriage/box on wheels; overcrowding; bucket as toilet; no longer treated as citizens or human beings; 7-day journey.
(c) Two points x 3 marks: screaming and shouting German voices; relentless barking (of dogs); the bright light.
(d) Explains biography and autobiography: 3 + 3 marks (only one explained: max 3 marks).
(e) Two reasons, each on a sliding scale of 3 (3 very good, 2 good/fair, 1 poor). Accept: importance of the Holocaust in history; he is a survivor/primary source who bears witness; to remember those who died; to counteract Holocaust denial.
(f) Sliding scale of 3: the organised murder of 6 million Jewish people by the Nazis during World War II.
(g) Two groups named: 3 + 3 marks. Explanations: 3 + 3 marks (sliding scale). Accept Roma people, disabled people, gay people, Jehovah's Witnesses, political enemies, pacifists, Slavic people.

prompt:
Write an account of one of the following:
(a) The League of Nations, 1920-1939.
(b) Hitler and the Jews, 1933-1939.
(c) Britain during World War II, 1939-1945.
model_answer:
(b) Hitler and the Jews, 1933-1939.
Hitler hated Jews. In Mein Kampf (1925) he said they were a race, not just a religion, and he blamed them for Germany losing World War One and for its money problems. The Nazis believed Aryan Germans were a master race.
When Hitler came to power in 1933, the Nazis did not yet plan to kill the Jews. They wanted to make life so hard that Jews would leave Germany. In April 1933 there was a boycott of Jewish shops and businesses, and Jews were pushed out of government jobs. Dachau, the first concentration camp, opened near Munich in 1933.
In 1935 the Nuremberg Laws took away Jews' German citizenship. Jews could not marry German citizens, hold government jobs or use parks. In 1937 Jews were banned from working as doctors and dentists. Nazi propaganda spread hatred of Jews through posters, films and newspapers.
On 9 November 1938, Kristallnacht (the Night of the Broken Glass), mobs wrecked Jewish homes, shops and schools and burned synagogues across Germany and Austria. About 90 Jews were killed and over 30,000 were sent to concentration camps. The Jewish community was even forced to pay for the damage.
Kristallnacht was a turning point: discrimination became open violence. Many Jews tried desperately to emigrate, but other countries took few immigrants and the Nazis taxed those who left. By 1939, when the war began, Jews in Germany had lost their rights, their jobs and their safety.

prompt:
Write an account of two of the following:
(a) Relations between the Irish government and the U.K., 1932-1939.
(b) Seán Lemass as Taoiseach, 1959-66.
(c) John Hume.
model_answer:
You only write two accounts. A model account for each option is given so you can pick.
(a) Relations between the Irish government and the U.K., 1932-1939.
Background: after 1922 the Irish Free State was still tied to Britain by the Anglo-Irish Treaty.
In 1932 Fianna Fáil, led by Éamon de Valera, came to power. He wanted to reduce British influence in Ireland. He removed the oath of allegiance to the British king.
De Valera stopped paying the land annuities to Britain. These were yearly repayments on loans that had helped Irish farmers buy their land. This started the Economic War (1932 to 1938).
Britain put taxes on Irish cattle and beef, and the Irish cattle trade almost collapsed. Ireland hit back with taxes on British coal, iron and steel. Both countries lost trade, and Irish farmers suffered most.
In 1937 de Valera brought in a new constitution, Bunreacht na hÉireann. The state was renamed Éire, and it claimed the whole island of Ireland.
In 1938 the Anglo-Irish Agreement ended the Economic War. Ireland paid a one-off £10 million instead of the £78 million owed, and both countries cancelled their tariffs.
Britain also handed back the treaty ports: Lough Swilly, Berehaven and Cobh. This was very important, because it meant Ireland could stay neutral in the coming World War Two (1939).
(b) Seán Lemass as Taoiseach, 1959-66.
Background: in the 1950s Ireland's economy was stuck because of protectionism (taxes on imports). About 40,000 people emigrated every year.
Lemass became Taoiseach in 1959. With T. K. Whitaker, whose report Economic Development (1958) said Ireland should choose free trade, he changed economic policy.
The First Programme for Economic Expansion (1958 to 1963) gave grants for exports and encouraged foreign firms to set up factories in Ireland.
It worked: the economy grew by about 4% a year, and emigration fell by 40%. Jobs were created and people's living standards rose.
In 1961 Teilifís Éireann, Ireland's first television service, began. It brought new ideas into Irish homes.
In 1965 Lemass signed the Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement with Britain, which removed tariffs on trade between the two countries. Ireland also applied to join the EEC.
Overall, Lemass modernised Ireland and made it more open to the world. He retired in 1966.
(c) John Hume.
John Hume was a Catholic nationalist from Derry. As a young man he became a key figure in the civil rights movement in Northern Ireland.
He supported NICRA (formed 1967), which wanted fair housing and jobs, 'one man, one vote' and an end to gerrymandering. He always believed in non-violent, peaceful protest.
In 1970 he helped found the SDLP, a nationalist party that wanted a united Ireland only by peaceful means and with the consent of the people.
He supported power-sharing between unionists and nationalists, as in the Sunningdale Agreement (1973), and the Anglo-Irish Agreement (1985), which gave Dublin a say in Northern Ireland.
He held talks with Gerry Adams of Sinn Féin, which helped lead to the IRA ceasefire of 1994.
He played a key part in the talks that led to the Good Friday Agreement in 1998, which set up a power-sharing Assembly.
In 1998 he and David Trimble won the Nobel Peace Prize for their work for peace.

Marked on the SRS (Significant Relevant Statement) principle: each SRS = 2 marks. For each account: max cumulative mark 8 + overall mark 2 (2 = very good/good, 1 = fair/poor, 0 = very poor). Two accounts: (8 + 2) x 2 = 20 marks.
(a) Material before 1932 counts as background: 1 SRS at most. Terms of the 1938 Anglo-Irish Agreement clearly stated: 1 SRS at most.

prompt: Write an account of life in Northern Ireland during World War Two. Refer to the economy and the Belfast Blitz in your answer.
model_answer:
Northern Ireland was part of the United Kingdom, so unlike Éire it was at war from 1939. Its government, led by Craig and then Andrews of the Ulster Unionist Party, fully supported the war effort.
The economy boomed. The Harland and Wolff shipyard built ships and Short Brothers built planes. Farmers grew more food and grew flax for linen parachutes and uniforms. Unemployment fell from 25% to 5%.
Northern Ireland's ports and airfields were used by the Allies, and up to 120,000 US troops were based there. About 38,000 people volunteered for the British forces.
In April and May 1941 German bombers attacked Belfast. This was the Belfast Blitz. The city was not ready: it lacked anti-aircraft guns and searchlights.
About 1,100 people were killed and 100,000 were made homeless. Many people left the city at night to sleep in fields and ditches, which was called ditching.
De Valera sent thirteen fire engines across the border to help put out the fires, even though Éire was neutral.

Expect points on both the economy (shipbuilding, aircraft, farming, US troops, unemployment falls) and the Belfast Blitz (date, lack of defences, deaths and homeless, ditching, fire engines from the South).

prompt: Say in your own words: what was détente?

prompt: Say in your own words: how did the Cold War end?
model_answer: Gorbachev became Soviet leader in 1985 when the economy was weak. His policies of glasnost and perestroika gave people more freedom, and Soviet troops stopped propping up communist governments. The Berlin Wall fell in 1989 and the USSR broke up in 1991.

Choose Topic 1 or 2 or 3:
Topic 1 - Rise of the Superpowers.
Write an account of a named major crisis in the Cold War between the USA and the USSR during the period 1945-1963.
model_answer:
The Cuban Missile Crisis, 1962.
Background: in 1959 Fidel Castro made Cuba communist and friendly with the USSR. Cuba is only about 90 miles from Florida. In 1961 a US-backed invasion of Cuba at the Bay of Pigs failed.
Soviet leader Khrushchev then secretly sent nuclear missiles to Cuba. These could hit most American cities.
On 14 October 1962 a US U2 spy plane photographed the missile launch sites being built in Cuba.
President Kennedy and his advisers decided not to bomb or invade Cuba, because that could start a nuclear war. Instead he set up a naval quarantine (blockade) around Cuba to stop Soviet ships bringing more missiles.
For thirteen days the world was on the edge of nuclear war, as Soviet ships sailed towards the US ships around Cuba.
On 28 October Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles. In return the USA promised not to invade Cuba, and in secret it also removed its own missiles from Turkey.
Result: a telephone hotline was set up to link Washington and Moscow, and the Nuclear Test Ban Treaty was signed in 1963.

model_answer:
A person who lived through the rise of the Superpowers (The Cold War): a mother living in West Berlin, 1948-1949.
My name is Greta and I live in West Berlin with my two children. After World War Two, Germany and Berlin were split into four zones. Our city sits deep inside the Soviet zone of East Germany, which is controlled by Stalin, the leader of the USSR.
In June 1948 Stalin closed all the roads, railways and canals into West Berlin. He wanted to starve us so that Britain, the USA and France would leave the city. Food and coal began to run out, and we were afraid that Soviet troops would take over.
Then the Western Allies started the Berlin Airlift. British and American planes flew in food, coal and medicine every day and night. The noise of the planes overhead never stopped, but to us it was the sound of hope. My children waited at the airport fence to watch them land.
The winter was hard. We had electricity for only a few hours a day and we were always hungry, but we never went without bread, thanks to the airlift.
In May 1949, after eleven months, Stalin gave up and lifted the blockade. Germany was then split into two countries, West Germany and East Germany, and NATO was set up to protect the West. Our city was saved, but Germany and Europe were now divided between the two superpowers.

prompt:
Winston Churchill gave this speech in Missouri, USA, on 5 March 1946. Read the extract and answer the questions which follow.
"From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent. Behind that line lie all the capitals of the ancient states of Central and Eastern Europe ... all are subject in one form or another, not only to Soviet influence but to a very high and, in many cases, increasing measure of control from Moscow."
(a) According to the source, what has descended across Europe?
(b) Give evidence from the source that Churchill believed eastern Europe was controlled by the USSR.
(c) Give one strength and one weakness of a speech as a historical source.
(d) Give two reasons why the Cold War began after World War Two.
(e) Explain two reasons why the Cold War came to an end by 1991.
model_answer:
(a) An iron curtain.
(b) He says the capitals of Central and Eastern Europe are subject "not only to Soviet influence" but to "increasing measure of control from Moscow".
(c) Strength: it is a primary source that tells us exactly what an important leader said and thought at the time. Weakness: it may be biased, because a speaker only gives his own side and wants to persuade his audience.
(d) First, the USA was capitalist and the USSR was communist, and each wanted its system to spread. Second, they did not trust each other: Stalin had signed the Nazi-Soviet Pact in 1939, and the USA dropped atomic bombs on Japan without telling Stalin.
(e) First, Gorbachev became Soviet leader in 1985 and brought in glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring), giving people more freedom. Second, the Soviet economy was weak, and Soviet troops stopped propping up communist governments in eastern Europe, so communism collapsed, the Berlin Wall fell in 1989 and the USSR broke up in 1991.

(a) Iron curtain: 3 marks.
(b) One piece of evidence from the source: 3 marks.
(c) One strength + one weakness: 3 + 3 marks.
(d) Two reasons, sliding scale of 3 each = 6 marks.
(e) Two reasons explained, sliding scale of 3 each = 6 marks (Gorbachev; glasnost/perestroika; weak Soviet economy; troops no longer propping up eastern European governments; fall of the Berlin Wall).

prompt:
Write an account of two of the following:
(a) Relations between the Irish government and the U.K., 1932-1939.
(b) Seán Lemass as Taoiseach, 1959-66.
(c) John Hume.
model_answer:
You only write two accounts. A model account for each option is given so you can pick.
(a) Relations between the Irish government and the U.K., 1932-1939.
Background: after 1922 the Irish Free State was still tied to Britain by the Anglo-Irish Treaty.
In 1932 Fianna Fáil, led by Éamon de Valera, came to power. He wanted to reduce British influence in Ireland. He removed the oath of allegiance to the British king.
De Valera stopped paying the land annuities to Britain. These were yearly repayments on loans that had helped Irish farmers buy their land. This started the Economic War (1932 to 1938).
Britain put taxes on Irish cattle and beef, and the Irish cattle trade almost collapsed. Ireland hit back with taxes on British coal, iron and steel. Both countries lost trade, and Irish farmers suffered most.
In 1937 de Valera brought in a new constitution, Bunreacht na hÉireann. The state was renamed Éire, and it claimed the whole island of Ireland.
In 1938 the Anglo-Irish Agreement ended the Economic War. Ireland paid a one-off £10 million instead of the £78 million owed, and both countries cancelled their tariffs.
Britain also handed back the treaty ports: Lough Swilly, Berehaven and Cobh. This was very important, because it meant Ireland could stay neutral in the coming World War Two (1939).
(b) Seán Lemass as Taoiseach, 1959-66.
Background: in the 1950s Ireland's economy was stuck because of protectionism (taxes on imports). About 40,000 people emigrated every year.
Lemass became Taoiseach in 1959. With T. K. Whitaker, whose report Economic Development (1958) said Ireland should choose free trade, he changed economic policy.
The First Programme for Economic Expansion (1958 to 1963) gave grants for exports and encouraged foreign firms to set up factories in Ireland.
It worked: the economy grew by about 4% a year, and emigration fell by 40%. Jobs were created and people's living standards rose.
In 1961 Teilifís Éireann, Ireland's first television service, began. It brought new ideas into Irish homes.
In 1965 Lemass signed the Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement with Britain, which removed tariffs on trade between the two countries. Ireland also applied to join the EEC.
Overall, Lemass modernised Ireland and made it more open to the world. He retired in 1966.
(c) John Hume.
John Hume was a Catholic nationalist from Derry. As a young man he became a key figure in the civil rights movement in Northern Ireland.
He supported NICRA (formed 1967), which wanted fair housing and jobs, 'one man, one vote' and an end to gerrymandering. He always believed in non-violent, peaceful protest.
In 1970 he helped found the SDLP, a nationalist party that wanted a united Ireland only by peaceful means and with the consent of the people.
He supported power-sharing between unionists and nationalists, as in the Sunningdale Agreement (1973), and the Anglo-Irish Agreement (1985), which gave Dublin a say in Northern Ireland.
He held talks with Gerry Adams of Sinn Féin, which helped lead to the IRA ceasefire of 1994.
He played a key part in the talks that led to the Good Friday Agreement in 1998, which set up a power-sharing Assembly.
In 1998 he and David Trimble won the Nobel Peace Prize for their work for peace.

Marked on the SRS (Significant Relevant Statement) principle: each SRS = 2 marks. For each account: max cumulative mark 8 + overall mark 2 (2 = very good/good, 1 = fair/poor, 0 = very poor). Two accounts: (8 + 2) x 2 = 20 marks.
(a) Material before 1932 counts as background: 1 SRS at most. Terms of the 1938 Anglo-Irish Agreement clearly stated: 1 SRS at most.

model_answer:

(c) First, music moved from vinyl records to cassettes, then CDs, then MP3 players like the iPod, so it became easier to carry music around. Second, today people stream almost any song instantly on a phone through services like Spotify, without buying a physical copy at all.

Choose Topic 1 or 2 or 3:

Write an account of the growth of the European Union since 1957.
model_answer:
The growth of the European Union since 1957.
Background: in 1957 six countries (France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg) signed the Treaty of Rome, creating the EEC. It aimed for a common market with no tariffs between members.
French President de Gaulle vetoed Britain's application in 1963 and 1967. After he resigned, the UK, Denmark and Ireland joined on 1 January 1973. In Ireland's referendum in 1972, 83.1% voted Yes.
More countries joined in the south of Europe: Greece in 1981, then Spain and Portugal in 1986.
In 1985 the Schengen Agreement allowed travel without border checks between many members (Ireland is not part of it).
The Single European Act (1986) created a single market, with free movement of goods, services, money and people.
The Maastricht Treaty (1993) turned the EEC into the European Union. It created EU citizenship and planned a single currency.
Austria, Finland and Sweden joined in 1995. The euro came into use in 2002 in the eurozone countries, including Ireland.
In 2004 ten countries joined, many of them former communist states in eastern Europe, and Croatia joined in 2013, bringing the EU to 28 members.
The Lisbon Treaty (2009) set out how a member could leave. In 2020 the UK became the first country to leave the EU (Brexit).

My name is Pierre and I work in a steel factory in Lorraine, in eastern France, near the German border. My father fought the Germans in World War One and I lived through the German occupation in World War Two. Our leaders said "never again".
In 1950 our foreign minister, Robert Schuman, announced a plan to put French and German coal and steel under one authority, so that war between us would be impossible. In 1951 the Treaty of Paris set up the European Coal and Steel Community with six countries. My factory now worked with German factories, not against them.
In 1957 the six countries signed the Treaty of Rome and created the EEC. Tariffs between the members were removed, so we could sell our goods more easily across Europe. Trade grew and so did our wages.
Under President Charles de Gaulle, France was a strong voice in the EEC. My cousin, a farmer, got guaranteed prices and grants from the Common Agricultural Policy, which began in 1963. De Gaulle did not trust Britain, so he vetoed its application in 1963 and 1967.
Outcome: after de Gaulle resigned, Britain, Ireland and Denmark joined in 1973. Over my lifetime the EEC grew into the European Union, with a single market and later the euro. Most of all, there has been peace between France and Germany ever since.

prompt:
Historian Tony Judt wrote about the early years of the EEC. Read the extract and answer the questions which follow.
"Intra-Community tariffs were removed by 1968, well ahead of schedule. Trade between the six member-states quadrupled in the same period. The farming workforce fell steadily, by some 4 per cent each year, while agricultural production per worker rose in the Sixties at an annual rate of 8.1 per cent." (Tony Judt, Postwar, 2005)
(a) According to the source, when were tariffs between member states removed?
(b) What happened to trade between the six member states?
(c) Name the EEC policy that helped farmers increase production.
(d) Why was the Treaty of Rome (1957) an important agreement?
(e) Write an account of how and why Ireland joined the EEC in 1973.
model_answer:
(a) By 1968, well ahead of schedule.
(b) It quadrupled (became four times bigger).
(c) The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP).
(d) The Treaty of Rome created the EEC with six countries. It set up a common market where members trade freely with no tariffs, which helped their economies grow. It also bound old enemies like France and Germany together, helping to keep the peace.
(e) Why: in the early 1950s, 90% of Irish exports went to Britain, and protectionism kept the economy small, with high unemployment and emigration. Seán Lemass and T. K. Whitaker moved Ireland towards free trade, and Lemass wanted Irish farmers to benefit from the CAP.
How: Ireland applied with Britain in 1961 and 1967, but both times de Gaulle vetoed Britain, so Ireland could not join. From 1970 Patrick Hillery led the entry talks; the Common Fisheries Policy was the main problem. In a referendum on 10 May 1972, 83.1% voted Yes. Ireland joined on 1 January 1973 with the UK and Denmark.

(b) Quadrupled: 3 marks.
(c) CAP: 3 marks.
(d) Two developed points, 3 + 3 marks (sliding scale).
(e) SRS principle: each significant relevant statement = 2 marks, max cumulative 8 + overall mark 2 = 10 marks. Should cover both why (trade with Britain, free trade, CAP) and how (1961 and 1967 applications, de Gaulle's veto, Hillery's talks, 1972 referendum, 1973 entry).

prompt:
Write an account of two of the following:
(a) Relations between the Irish government and the U.K., 1932-1939.
(b) Seán Lemass as Taoiseach, 1959-66.
(c) John Hume.
model_answer:
You only write two accounts. A model account for each option is given so you can pick.
(a) Relations between the Irish government and the U.K., 1932-1939.
Background: after 1922 the Irish Free State was still tied to Britain by the Anglo-Irish Treaty.
In 1932 Fianna Fáil, led by Éamon de Valera, came to power. He wanted to reduce British influence in Ireland. He removed the oath of allegiance to the British king.
De Valera stopped paying the land annuities to Britain. These were yearly repayments on loans that had helped Irish farmers buy their land. This started the Economic War (1932 to 1938).
Britain put taxes on Irish cattle and beef, and the Irish cattle trade almost collapsed. Ireland hit back with taxes on British coal, iron and steel. Both countries lost trade, and Irish farmers suffered most.
In 1937 de Valera brought in a new constitution, Bunreacht na hÉireann. The state was renamed Éire, and it claimed the whole island of Ireland.
In 1938 the Anglo-Irish Agreement ended the Economic War. Ireland paid a one-off £10 million instead of the £78 million owed, and both countries cancelled their tariffs.
Britain also handed back the treaty ports: Lough Swilly, Berehaven and Cobh. This was very important, because it meant Ireland could stay neutral in the coming World War Two (1939).
(b) Seán Lemass as Taoiseach, 1959-66.
Background: in the 1950s Ireland's economy was stuck because of protectionism (taxes on imports). About 40,000 people emigrated every year.
Lemass became Taoiseach in 1959. With T. K. Whitaker, whose report Economic Development (1958) said Ireland should choose free trade, he changed economic policy.
The First Programme for Economic Expansion (1958 to 1963) gave grants for exports and encouraged foreign firms to set up factories in Ireland.
It worked: the economy grew by about 4% a year, and emigration fell by 40%. Jobs were created and people's living standards rose.
In 1961 Teilifís Éireann, Ireland's first television service, began. It brought new ideas into Irish homes.
In 1965 Lemass signed the Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement with Britain, which removed tariffs on trade between the two countries. Ireland also applied to join the EEC.
Overall, Lemass modernised Ireland and made it more open to the world. He retired in 1966.
(c) John Hume.
John Hume was a Catholic nationalist from Derry. As a young man he became a key figure in the civil rights movement in Northern Ireland.
He supported NICRA (formed 1967), which wanted fair housing and jobs, 'one man, one vote' and an end to gerrymandering. He always believed in non-violent, peaceful protest.
In 1970 he helped found the SDLP, a nationalist party that wanted a united Ireland only by peaceful means and with the consent of the people.
He supported power-sharing between unionists and nationalists, as in the Sunningdale Agreement (1973), and the Anglo-Irish Agreement (1985), which gave Dublin a say in Northern Ireland.
He held talks with Gerry Adams of Sinn Féin, which helped lead to the IRA ceasefire of 1994.
He played a key part in the talks that led to the Good Friday Agreement in 1998, which set up a power-sharing Assembly.
In 1998 he and David Trimble won the Nobel Peace Prize for their work for peace.
marking_scheme:
Marked on the SRS (Significant Relevant Statement) principle: each SRS = 2 marks. For each account: max cumulative mark 8 + overall mark 2 (2 = very good/good, 1 = fair/poor, 0 = very poor). Two accounts: (8 + 2) x 2 = 20 marks.
(a) Material before 1932 counts as background: 1 SRS at most. Terms of the 1938 Anglo-Irish Agreement clearly stated: 1 SRS at most.

Sutton worked back to the start of the Troubles in 1969 and continued recording killings during the 1990s. Sutton's index stops at 2001. 2. Court records: they would give details of who carried out a killing, and how and why it happened.

prompt: Identify a significant event that happened during the Northern Ireland Troubles. Write an account of the event and explain why it was significant.
model_answer:
Event: Bloody Sunday, 30 January 1972.
In August 1971 the British army had begun internment (prison without trial). Over 90% of internees were nationalists, so many Catholics were angry.
NICRA organised a march in Derry on 30 January 1972 to protest against internment.
British soldiers opened fire on the marchers and shot dead thirteen unarmed people.
Why it was significant: nationalists were furious. Protesters burned the British Embassy in Dublin, and many young men joined the IRA, so the violence got worse.
In March 1972 Britain closed Stormont and brought in direct rule from London. 1972 became the worst year of the Troubles, with almost 500 deaths.

model_answer: Women did not have to serve on juries after 1927. The marriage bar forced women to give up jobs when they married, and contraceptives were banned in 1935. The 1937 Constitution stressed women's duties in the home.

prompt: Say in your own words: what was the Irish Women's Liberation Movement?
model_answer: The IWLM began in 1970 to campaign for women's rights. Its pamphlet Chains or Change was launched on The Late Late Show. Members took the "contraceptive train" to Belfast in protest.

prompt: Say in your own words: name two changes in the 1970s that improved women's rights.
model_answer: Joining the EEC in 1973 meant equal pay for equal work, and the marriage bar was removed. The Employment Equality Act (1977) banned gender discrimination at work.

prompt: Say in your own words: name one woman who made history in twentieth-century Ireland and what she did.
model_answer: Mary Robinson became Ireland's first woman president in 1990. Her election showed how much women's place in Irish public life had changed.

The GAA is an example of a sporting, cultural or social movement that impacted on Irish life. Examine the two photographs below and answer the questions which follow.

model_answer:
(a) 104 years (2019 - 1915).
(b) 1. Clothing: in 1915 the players wear long skirts, blouses and ties; in 2019 they wear fitted jerseys, shorts and socks made for sport.
2. Head gear: in 1915 no one wears a helmet; in 2019 the players wear helmets with face guards for safety.
3. Sponsorship and surroundings: the 2019 jerseys have sponsor logos and the match is in a big stadium, Croke Park, with a full stand; in 1915 there are no sponsors and the match is on a rough field with people standing around the edge.
(c) 1. Women played camogie in both 1915 and 2019, so women's interest in the game has continued.
2. Both photos show players using hurleys and a sliotar, and the two teams wear different tops, so the basic game is the same. (Also: spectators came to watch in both.)
marking_scheme:
(a) 104 years: 3 marks.
(b) Three differences x 3 marks = 9 marks. Points must clearly refer to one or both photographs: players' clothing, head gear, sponsorship, nature of play, surroundings.
(c) Two points of continuity x 3 marks = 6 marks: women's interest in camogie; spectator interest in both; teams differentiated by different tops in both; similar hurleys and sliotars.
Total 18 marks.

prompt:
Read this extract from Chains or Change, the manifesto of the Irish Women's Liberation Movement (1971), and answer the questions which follow.
"Irishwomen in the home have noticeably inferior status. And then of course, if the woman wishes, or needs, to go out to work, she runs into unequal pay, the marriage bar, no amenities and penalising taxation."
(a) Give two problems, mentioned in the source, for women who wanted to go out to work.
(b) What was the marriage bar?
(c) Describe two ways women's lives changed in Ireland in the 1970s.
(d) Write a short account of the campaign for women's suffrage in Ireland before 1922.
model_answer:
(a) Unequal pay and the marriage bar (also: no amenities, penalising taxation).
(b) The marriage bar was a rule that made women give up jobs, such as in the civil service, when they got married.
(c) First, when Ireland joined the EEC in 1973 it had to give equal pay for equal work, and the marriage bar was removed for civil servants. Second, the Employment Equality Act (1977) banned gender discrimination at work, and from 1976 women had an equal duty to serve on juries.
(d) In 1900 women could not vote in parliamentary elections. In 1908 Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington and Margaret Cousins founded the Irish Women's Franchise League (IWFL). They wrote letters, gave speeches and collected signatures, and in 1912 started a newspaper, The Irish Citizen. When the Home Rule Bill left out votes for women, suffragettes smashed windows in Dublin Castle. Jailed suffragettes went on hunger strike, and the Cat and Mouse Act (1913) let them out to recover and then arrested them again. Women's war work in World War One won support, and in 1918 women over thirty who owned property got the vote. Constance Markievicz became the first woman elected to Westminster. In 1922 the Free State Constitution gave the vote to all citizens over twenty-one.
marking_scheme:
(a) Two problems from the source, 3 + 3 marks.
(b) Clear explanation: 3 marks.
(c) Two developed changes, sliding scale of 3 each = 6 marks (equal pay, marriage bar removed, Employment Equality Act, juries, contraception).
(d) SRS principle: each significant relevant statement = 2 marks, max cumulative 8 + overall mark 2 = 10 marks.

prompt: What is a hypothesis?
options: A prediction that can be tested
A list of results from an experiment
A graph of the data collected
A summary written at the end
explanation: A hypothesis is a prediction that can be tested by an investigation. It is often written as "If ... then ...".

prompt: Which of these is written as a testable hypothesis?
options: Does salt change how water boils?
Salt is a white crystalline solid.
If salt is added to water, then its boiling point will rise.
Water boils in a beaker on a tripod.
explanation: A hypothesis is a statement that can be tested, often "If ... then ...". A question is not a hypothesis.

prompt: What is a prediction?
options: A measurement taken with a ruler
A suggestion of what might happen
A rule that is always true
A check done by other scientists
explanation: A prediction is a suggestion of what you think will happen. If it can be tested, it is a hypothesis.

prompt: What is a control in an investigation?
options: The person in charge of the lab
The safety rules for the lab
A set-up identical to the test except for the one thing being tested
explanation: A control is a comparison. It is the same as the investigation in every way except for the one factor being tested.

prompt: What is the independent variable?
explanation: The independent variable is the one thing you change on purpose, such as the mass of salt added.

prompt: What is the dependent variable?
options: The thing you keep the same
explanation: The dependent variable is what you measure to see if it responds to the change, such as the boiling temperature.

prompt: Why are controlled variables kept the same?
options: To make the graph look neater
To make the experiment finish faster
So that it is a fair test
So that you need less equipment
explanation: Keeping everything else the same means only one thing is changed. That makes it a fair test.

prompt: On a line graph, where does the independent variable go?
explanation: The independent variable (what you change) goes on the x-axis. The dependent variable goes on the y-axis.

prompt: A student tests how salt affects boiling point. Which should be kept the same?
explanation: The volume of water is a controlled variable. The mass of salt is changed, and the boiling temperature is measured.

prompt: Which is a safe way to heat a liquid in a test tube?
options: Point the open end towards your partner
Point the open end away from yourself and others
Hold the test tube in your bare hand
Leave the Bunsen burner lit and walk away
explanation: Always point a heated test tube away from yourself and others, in case the liquid spits out.

prompt: What is a hazard?
options: A result that does not fit the pattern
explanation: A hazard is something that can cause harm, such as fire, chemicals, broken glass, electricity or spills.

prompt: Which of these is quantitative data?
explanation: Quantitative data uses numbers. "20 °C" is a number with a unit.

prompt: What is qualitative data?
options: Data that describes without using numbers
Data shown only on a pie chart
Data that has been checked by experts
explanation: Qualitative data describes things, such as colour or smell, without using numbers.

prompt: Where do you read the volume in a graduated cylinder?
options: At the top of the meniscus
At the bottom of the meniscus
At the top of the cylinder
explanation: Read a graduated cylinder at eye level, at the bottom of the curved surface (the meniscus).

prompt: Setting a balance to zero before using it is called what?
explanation: To calibrate equipment means to set it correctly before use, for example setting a balance to zero.

prompt: What is the resolution of a measuring instrument?
options: The largest value it can show
The number of times you use it
The smallest change it can detect
explanation: Resolution is the smallest change an instrument can detect. A ruler marked in mm has a resolution of 1 mm.

prompt: Why should you take at least three readings?
options: To make the results more reliable
To make the experiment more dangerous
explanation: Repeating readings and finding the mean makes results more reliable. One odd reading has less effect.

prompt: Readings are 4, 5 and 6. What is the mean?
explanation: Add the readings (4 + 5 + 6 = 15) and divide by how many there are (3). 15 ÷ 3 = 5.

prompt: Readings are 12, 15, 9 and 14. What is the range?
explanation: The range is the largest minus the smallest value: 15 − 9 = 6.

prompt: What are precise results?
options: Results that are all far apart
Results that are written in pen
Results that are close to the mean
explanation: Precise results are close to each other and close to the mean.

prompt: Which graph should you use for separate categories, such as eye colour?
explanation: A bar chart is used for separate categories. Leave gaps between the bars.

prompt: What does a Sankey diagram show?
options: Amounts of energy, using the width of arrows
explanation: In a Sankey diagram the width of each arrow shows the amount of energy. It is named after Matthew Sankey.

prompt: What does "directly proportional" look like on a graph?
options: A straight line through the origin
explanation: When two things are directly proportional, both increase together, giving a straight line through the origin (0, 0).

prompt: As the distance from a lamp increases, the number of bubbles goes down. What kind of relationship is this?
explanation: In an inverse relationship, as one variable increases, the other decreases.

prompt: What must a conclusion do?
options: Match the data and say if the hypothesis is supported
Repeat the method step by step
Give the name of every student
explanation: A conclusion sums up what was found. It must match the data and support or contradict the hypothesis.

prompt: What is included in an evaluation?
options: Only the title of the investigation
Odd results, difficulties and how to improve it
explanation: An evaluation looks back at the whole investigation. It explains odd results and suggests improvements.

prompt: What is peer review?
options: Checking a graph has a title
Other experts reading and checking the work
explanation: Peer review is when other scientists check the work before it is trusted. It acts as quality control.

prompt: What does bias mean in a source of information?
options: It gives only one point of view
explanation: A biased source gives only one side of a story and ignores other views.

prompt: Which website is most likely to be reliable?
options: A government site that names its authors and sources
A shop selling the product it praises
A page with no author and no date
A post from an anonymous account
explanation: A credible source names the author, gives dates and sources, and is often from a university, government or NASA.

prompt: Why do scientific ideas change over time?
options: Scientists get bored of old ideas
explanation: New investigations can give new evidence. An old hypothesis may then be replaced by a new one.

prompt: Say in your own words: what is the difference between a prediction and a hypothesis?
model_answer: A prediction is a suggestion of what might happen. A hypothesis is a prediction that can be tested by an investigation. It is often written as "If ... then ...".

prompt: Say in your own words: what are the independent, dependent and controlled variables?
model_answer: The independent variable is the one thing you change. The dependent variable is what you measure. The controlled variables are everything else, which you keep the same.

prompt: Explain what a control is and why it is used.
model_answer: A control is a set-up that is identical to the investigation except for the one thing being tested. It lets you compare, so you know the result is caused by that one thing.

prompt: Why do scientists repeat readings and calculate the mean?
model_answer: Repeating readings makes results more reliable. Taking the mean (average) reduces the effect of one odd or wrong reading.

prompt: Give three rules for drawing a good line graph.
model_answer: Use a sharp pencil. Put the independent variable on the x-axis and the dependent variable on the y-axis, and label both axes with units. Draw a line through as many points as possible.

prompt: What is the difference between a conclusion and an evaluation?
model_answer: A conclusion sums up the findings and says if they support the hypothesis. An evaluation looks back at the whole investigation, explains odd results and suggests improvements.

prompt: What is peer review, and why is it useful?
model_answer: Peer review is when other experts read and check a scientist's work. It acts as quality control, so the work can be trusted.

prompt: Give two signs that a website is a reliable source of science information.
model_answer: It names the author and gives dates and sources. It is from a trusted organisation such as a university, the government or NASA, and it is not trying to sell you something.

prompt: Name three safety rules for working in the school laboratory.
model_answer: Wear a lab coat and safety glasses, and tie long hair back. Point a heated test tube away from people. Never handle broken glass with bare hands and report spills to the teacher.

Mass of salt (g) | Boiling point (°C) | | | | | Average boiling point (°C)
0 | 100 | 101 | 100 | 100 | 102 | 100.6
2 | 101 | 104 | 101 | 100 | 103 | 101.8
4 | 103 | 105 | 104 | 106 | 107 |
6 | 106 | 108 | 107 | 107 | 108 | 107.2

model_answer:

prompt:

UCC Study: High fibre foods ease stress effects
Interest has been growing in recent years in the link between gut bacteria and stress-related disorders. Researchers at University College Cork (UCC) have shown that micro-organisms in the gut (intestines) are really important for our brain health.
[Picture: bacteria in the gut]

Using behavioural tests, the mice were assessed for anxiety and depressive-like behaviour. Coronavirus disease (COVID-19) is an infectious disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. prompt: What is an organism?
explanation: An organism is any living thing, such as a plant, an animal or a bacterium.

prompt: Which of these is one of the five characteristics of all living things?
explanation: All living things are made of cells and carry out nutrition, excretion, response and reproduction.

prompt: A rabbit eating lettuce is an example of which characteristic of life?
explanation: Nutrition is how living things get their food.

prompt: What is excretion?
options: How living things react to changes
How living things make new living things
How living things get their food
How living things get rid of the wastes they make
explanation: Excretion is getting rid of the waste products made in the body, such as carbon dioxide.

prompt: A plant growing towards light is an example of which characteristic?
explanation: Response is how living things react to changes around them. The plant reacts to light.

prompt: Mushrooms, moulds and yeast belong to which group of living things?
explanation: Mushrooms, moulds and yeast are all fungi.

prompt: Seaweeds and amoeba are placed in which group?
explanation: Seaweeds and amoeba belong to the "others" group, called protists.

prompt: What is a vertebrate?
options: A tiny living thing that causes decay
explanation: A vertebrate has a backbone, for example a horse, a frog or a seagull.

prompt: Which of these animals is an invertebrate?
explanation: An earthworm has no backbone, so it is an invertebrate. The others are vertebrates.

prompt: What does biodiversity mean?
options: The number of cells in a body
The range of different living things in an area
explanation: Biodiversity is the range (variety) of different living things in an area.

prompt: Which human activity reduces biodiversity?
explanation: Clearing woodland destroys the conditions that living things need, so fewer kinds can live there.

prompt: How do living things grow?
options: Cells join together into one cell
Cells divide to make more cells
explanation: Cells divide to form two cells. This cell division is how living things grow.

prompt: What is the single cell that a human grows from called?
explanation: A human grows from a single cell called a zygote.

prompt: Which part of a cell controls what goes in and out?
explanation: The cell membrane is a thin layer around the cell. It controls what passes in and out.

prompt: What is the cytoplasm?
options: The control centre of the cell
A hard outer layer of cellulose
The watery liquid between the nucleus and the membrane
A green structure that makes food
explanation: Cytoplasm is the watery liquid in the cell. Some cell reactions happen there.

prompt: What do mitochondria do?
explanation: Mitochondria are tiny structures that supply energy to the cell by respiration.

prompt: Which part of the cell is its control centre?
explanation: The nucleus controls the cell. It holds the chromosomes.

prompt: What is a gene?
options: A thin layer around the cell
A piece of DNA that controls one feature
explanation: Chromosomes carry many genes. Each gene is made of DNA and controls one feature.

prompt: How many chromosomes are in a human body cell?
explanation: Human body cells have 46 chromosomes. Sperm and egg cells have 23.

prompt: Which part is found in plant cells but NOT in animal cells?
explanation: The cell wall, the large vacuole and chloroplasts are found in plant cells only.

prompt: What is the cell wall made of?
explanation: The cell wall is made of cellulose. It gives the plant cell strength.

prompt: What does a full vacuole do for a plant cell?
options: It pushes out on the wall and makes the cell firm
explanation: The vacuole holds liquid. When it is full it pushes against the wall and makes the cell firm.

prompt: What do chloroplasts contain?
explanation: Chloroplasts contain green chlorophyll. They make food by photosynthesis.

prompt: Which part of a microscope holds the objective lenses?
explanation: The objective lenses sit on the rotating nosepiece.

prompt: Which focus knob should you use at high power?
explanation: Use the coarse focus at low power and the fine focus at high power.

prompt: The eyepiece is ×10 and the objective lens is ×40. What is the total magnification?
explanation: Total magnification = eyepiece × objective = 10 × 40 = ×400.

prompt: Which stain is used to show up the nucleus in cheek cells?
explanation: Methylene blue is used for cheek cells. Iodine solution is used for onion cells.

prompt: Why is the cover slip lowered at an angle of 45 degrees?
explanation: Lowering the cover slip slowly at 45 degrees stops air bubbles being trapped.

prompt: Which stain is used for onion cells?
explanation: Iodine solution stains the nucleus of onion cells.

prompt: List the five characteristics of all living things.
model_answer: All living things are made of cells. They carry out nutrition (getting food), excretion (getting rid of waste), response (reacting to changes) and reproduction (making new living things).

prompt: Name the five main groups of living things, with one example of each.
model_answer: Bacteria (e.g. bacteria that cause decay), fungi (mushrooms), plants (trees), animals (humans) and others called protists (seaweed or amoeba).

prompt: What is the difference between a vertebrate and an invertebrate? Give an example of each.
model_answer: A vertebrate has a backbone, such as a frog. An invertebrate has no backbone, such as a spider.

prompt: Name the parts of an animal cell and say what each one does.
model_answer: The cell membrane controls what goes in and out. The cytoplasm is the watery liquid where some reactions happen. The nucleus is the control centre and holds the chromosomes.

prompt: Name three parts found only in plant cells and say what each does.
model_answer: The cell wall is made of cellulose and gives strength. The vacuole holds liquid and keeps the cell firm. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and make food by photosynthesis.

prompt: Say in your own words how the nucleus controls the cell.
model_answer: The nucleus contains strands called chromosomes. Each chromosome carries many genes, made of DNA. Each gene controls one feature.

prompt: How do you work out the total magnification of a microscope? Give an example.
model_answer: Multiply the power of the eyepiece lens by the power of the objective lens. For example ×10 × ×20 = ×200.

prompt: Describe how to prepare a slide of cheek cells.
model_answer: Gently scrape the inside of your cheek with a cotton bud and smear it on a slide. Add a few drops of methylene blue. Lower a cover slip at 45 degrees and soak up extra stain with tissue paper. View with the lowest power lens first.

prompt: What is biodiversity, and how can humans reduce it?
model_answer: Biodiversity is the range of different living things in an area. Humans reduce it by clearing woodland for houses and roads, cutting forests and polluting lakes.

prompt: What is asexual reproduction?
options: Making new living things from one parent only
Joining a sperm and an egg
Making new living things from two parents
explanation: Asexual reproduction needs only one parent. No sex cells join together.

prompt: Why are offspring from asexual reproduction identical to the parent?
options: They get exact copies of the parent's genes
They grow in the same place
They have genes from two parents
explanation: With only one parent, the offspring get exact copies of that parent's genes.

prompt: Which is an example of asexual reproduction?
options: A bird laying a fertilised egg
explanation: Strawberry runners grow into new plants identical to the parent. No sex cells are involved.

prompt: How do bacteria reproduce?
explanation: Bacteria divide in two to form two identical cells. This is asexual reproduction.

prompt: What is a gamete?
options: A sex cell, such as a sperm or an egg
explanation: A gamete is a sex cell. Sperm and egg cells are gametes.

prompt: What is fertilisation?
explanation: Fertilisation is when two gametes (sex cells) join together.

prompt: What is formed when a sperm and an egg join?
explanation: Two gametes join to form a single cell called a zygote.

prompt: What is the main benefit of sexual reproduction?
options: It is faster than asexual reproduction
Offspring are identical to the parent
Offspring have features of both parents, so they vary
explanation: Offspring get genes from two parents, so they are not identical. This variation is the main benefit.

prompt: What does variation mean?
options: Differences between living things of the same kind
Living things that are exactly the same
The number of chromosomes in a cell
explanation: Variation means differences between living things of the same kind, such as different eye colours.

prompt: Which is an inherited characteristic?
explanation: Eye colour is passed on by genes. The others are learned skills.

prompt: Which is an example of non-inherited (acquired) variation?
options: Being able to ride a bike
explanation: Riding a bike is learned and practised. It is not passed on by genes.

prompt: Where are chromosomes found?
explanation: Chromosomes are thread-like structures found in the nucleus of each cell.

prompt: How many chromosomes are in most human body cells?
explanation: Most human cells have 46 chromosomes. Sex cells have half that number, 23.

prompt: How many chromosomes are in a human sperm cell?
explanation: Sex cells (gametes) have 23 chromosomes, half the number in body cells.

prompt: What are chromosomes made of?
explanation: Chromosomes are made of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and protein.

prompt: What is a gene?
options: A short section of DNA that controls a characteristic
explanation: Genes are short sections of DNA on chromosomes. Each controls an inherited characteristic.

prompt: What does a dominant gene do?
options: It stops the other version of the gene from working
It only shows if there are two copies
It is always written in small letters
It is only found in sex cells
explanation: A dominant gene (capital letter) shows and stops the recessive version from working.

prompt: When does a recessive characteristic show?
options: When there is one dominant gene
Only when there is no dominant gene
explanation: A recessive gene only shows when there is no dominant version, e.g. bb.

prompt: What is a genotype?
options: The genes an organism has, e.g. Bb
explanation: The genotype is the genes an organism has. The phenotype is what it looks like.

prompt: B = brown eyes (dominant), b = blue eyes. What is the phenotype of a person who is Bb?
explanation: B is dominant, so one B is enough for brown eyes.

prompt: A parent is Bb. Which gametes can this parent make?
explanation: Each gamete carries one version of each gene, so a Bb parent makes B or b gametes.

prompt: What is the chance of a blue-eyed (bb) child if both parents are Bb?
explanation: Bb × Bb gives BB, Bb, Bb and bb. Only 1 in 4 is bb, so the chance is 25%.

prompt: A BB parent and a bb parent have children. What will all the children be?
explanation: The BB parent can only pass on B and the bb parent only b, so every child is Bb (brown).

prompt: What is a Punnett square?
options: A grid that shows all possible offspring of a cross
explanation: A Punnett square is a grid used in a genetic cross to show all the possible offspring.

prompt: In a pedigree chart, what does a square stand for?
explanation: A square is a male and a circle is a female.

prompt: In a pedigree chart, what does a shaded (solid) symbol mean?
options: The person is affected by the condition
explanation: A solid symbol shows an affected person. An empty symbol is unaffected.

prompt: What is a carrier?
options: A person with two dominant genes
A person with one copy of a recessive gene who does not show the condition
A person with no genes for the condition
explanation: A carrier has one copy of the recessive gene but does not show the condition. They can pass it on.

prompt: Say in your own words: what is asexual reproduction? Give an example.
model_answer: Asexual reproduction makes new living things from one parent only, with no sex cells joining. The offspring are identical to the parent. Example: strawberry plants growing runners, or bacteria dividing in two.

prompt: Describe sexual reproduction, using the words gamete, fertilisation and zygote.
model_answer: Each parent makes gametes (sex cells), such as sperm and eggs. Fertilisation is when two gametes join. This forms a single cell called a zygote, which grows into the new living thing.

prompt: Give two differences between sexual and asexual reproduction.
model_answer: Sexual reproduction needs two parents, but asexual needs only one. In sexual reproduction the offspring vary, but in asexual reproduction they are identical to the parent.

prompt: Explain the difference between inherited and non-inherited variation, with an example of each.
model_answer: Inherited variation is passed on by genes, e.g. eye colour. Non-inherited variation is learned or practised, e.g. speaking a language or riding a bike.

prompt: Explain how chromosomes, DNA and genes are linked.
model_answer: Chromosomes are thread-like structures in the nucleus. They are made of DNA and protein. Genes are short sections of DNA on a chromosome, and each one controls a characteristic.

prompt: Say in your own words what dominant and recessive mean.
model_answer: A dominant gene shows itself and stops the other version working. It is written with a capital letter. A recessive gene only shows when there is no dominant gene, e.g. bb.

prompt: What is the difference between genotype and phenotype?
model_answer: The genotype is the genes an organism has, for example Bb. The phenotype is what it looks like, for example brown eyes.

prompt: Explain what the symbols in a pedigree chart mean.
model_answer: A circle is a female and a square is a male. A shaded symbol is an affected person and an empty symbol is unaffected. A horizontal line joins a couple and a vertical line goes down to their children.

prompt: What is a species?
options: A group of living things that can reproduce together and have offspring that can also reproduce
Any animal that lives in the same habitat
A living thing that has died out
explanation: Members of a species can breed together and their young can also breed.

prompt: Why are a cat and a rabbit different species?
explanation: Living things that cannot reproduce together to make fertile offspring are different species.

prompt: What is a mutation?
explanation: A mutation is a change in a gene. It can cause new inherited variation.

prompt: Which is an example of the effect of a mutation?
options: A tree losing its leaves in autumn
A dog being trained to sit
A person born with extra toes
explanation: Most humans have five toes. If the gene is altered (a mutation), a person may have extra toes.

prompt: What two things cause genes to differ between members of a species?
explanation: Mutations and sexual reproduction mix and change genes, causing inherited variation.

prompt: What is evolution?
options: New kinds of living things developing from earlier forms over a long time
An animal changing during its own life
explanation: Evolution is how new kinds of living things develop from earlier forms by genetic changes over long periods.

prompt: Who put forward the theory of evolution by natural selection?
explanation: Charles Darwin put forward the theory in 1859, working with Alfred Russel Wallace.

prompt: In what year did Darwin publish his theory of natural selection?
explanation: Darwin put forward his theory of evolution by natural selection in 1859.

prompt: Which of these did Darwin notice?
options: Living things produce huge numbers of offspring
All members of a species are identical
The environment can support unlimited living things
explanation: Darwin saw that living things produce many offspring, but the environment can only support a limited number.

prompt: What did Darwin call the competition between living things for scarce resources?
explanation: Living things must compete for scarce resources like food, water, light and space. Darwin called this the struggle for existence.

prompt: What is an adaptation?
options: A disease that kills a species
A characteristic that helps an organism survive and reproduce
explanation: An adaptation is a feature that helps a living thing survive and reproduce in its habitat.

prompt: In natural selection, which organisms are most likely to survive?
options: Those best suited (adapted) to their environment
explanation: Nature selects the organisms best adapted to their environment. They survive and pass on their genes.

prompt: What happens to badly adapted organisms in natural selection?
options: They may die and not pass on their genes
They always have the most young
They change their genes on purpose
They become a new species straight away
explanation: Badly adapted organisms are less likely to survive, so they do not pass on their genes.

prompt: Why were light peppered moths common before 1760?
options: They were faster than dark moths
They were hidden on lichen-covered bark
Birds did not eat moths then
explanation: Light moths were camouflaged on pale, lichen-covered bark, so birds did not see them.

prompt: Why did dark peppered moths become common by the 1860s?
options: Light moths moved to another country
Pollution made the bark dark, so light moths were seen and eaten
The moths were painted by scientists
explanation: Pollution killed the lichens and darkened the bark. Light moths were easy to spot and were eaten.

prompt: What was different about the finches on each Galápagos island?
explanation: Darwin saw that the finches' beak shapes differed from island to island, to suit the food there.

prompt: How did many finch species come from one species?
options: On each island, birds with the beak best suited to the food survived and passed it on
The finches chose to change their beaks
Each finch flew in from a different continent
explanation: Natural selection on each island favoured the best beak for that food. Over time new species evolved.

prompt: How does evolution lead to biodiversity?
options: It makes all living things the same
Over time it produces many new species
It stops living things from changing
explanation: As new species evolve over long periods, the variety of living things (biodiversity) increases.

prompt: About how old is the Earth?
explanation: Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago.

prompt: Where was the first life on Earth found?
explanation: The first life was bacteria in the sea, about 3.8 billion years ago.

prompt: Which appeared on Earth most recently?
explanation: Humans appeared only about 200 000 years ago. Land plants came 500 million years ago.

prompt: What does extinct mean?
options: A living thing that is very common
A type of living thing that has died out completely
An animal that has been tamed
explanation: An extinct living thing has died out and no longer exists, like the dinosaurs.

prompt: What is a fossil?
options: The remains of a very ancient living thing
explanation: A fossil is the remains of a living thing from a very long time ago.

prompt: Say in your own words: what is a species?
model_answer: A species is a group of living things that can reproduce together. Their offspring can also reproduce. For example, all dogs are one species.

prompt: What is a mutation, and why is it important for evolution?
model_answer: A mutation is a change in a gene. It causes new inherited variation, and some new variations may help a living thing survive.

prompt: What did Darwin observe that led to his theory?
model_answer: Living things produce huge numbers of offspring. The environment can only support a limited number. Members of a species vary. So they must compete for scarce resources (the struggle for existence).

prompt: Outline the theory of evolution by natural selection in your own words.
model_answer: Members of a species show variation. They compete for scarce resources. Those best adapted to their environment survive and reproduce, passing on their useful genes. Over many generations the species changes.

prompt: What is an adaptation? Give an example.
model_answer: An adaptation is a characteristic that helps a living thing survive and reproduce. For example, a finch with a short, strong beak can crack hard seeds.

prompt: Explain how peppered moths are an example of natural selection.
model_answer: Pollution killed lichens and darkened tree bark. Light moths were easily seen and eaten by birds, but dark moths were hidden. Dark moths survived and passed on their genes, so by the 1860s most moths were dark.

prompt: Explain how many finch species evolved on the Galápagos Islands.
model_answer: One species of finch arrived from South America. On each island, birds with the beak best suited to the food there survived and passed on their beak shape. Over a long time many new finch species evolved.

prompt: Describe the timeline of life on Earth in three or four steps.
model_answer: Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago. The first life, bacteria in the sea, appeared about 3.8 billion years ago. Land plants came about 500 million years ago and dinosaurs 220 million years ago. Humans appeared only 200 000 years ago.

prompt:
Before 1760 most peppered moths in the north of England were light coloured. Pollution during the Industrial Revolution killed the lichens on tree bark, and the bark became dark. By the 1860s most of the moths were dark coloured.
(a) Why were light-coloured moths hard to see before 1760?
(b) Suggest what happened to light-coloured moths after the bark became dark.
(c) Explain how the change in the moths is evidence for natural selection.
(d) Pollution controls have now let the lichens grow back. Predict the colour of most moths today. Give a reason.
model_answer:
(a) They were camouflaged against the pale, lichen-covered bark.
(b) They stood out on the dark bark, so birds saw them and ate them.
(c) The dark moths were better adapted to the dark bark. They survived and passed on their genes for dark colour, so over time most moths became dark.
(d) Light coloured. On pale bark, light moths are hidden again, so they survive better and pass on their genes.
marking_scheme:
(a) Camouflage / matched the lichen-covered bark (3 marks).
(b) Easily seen and eaten by birds (3 marks).
(c) Better-adapted (dark) moths survived and reproduced, passing on their genes (3 marks).
(d) Light (1 mark) + light moths camouflaged again so they survive (2 marks).

prompt:
Darwin found many types of finch on the Galápagos Islands. They had different beak shapes.
(a) What is meant by a species?
(b) A finch with a short, strong beak lives on an island with lots of hard seeds. Explain why this beak is an adaptation.
(c) Explain how one type of finch could evolve into many different species over a long time.
(d) What is a mutation, and why are mutations important for evolution?
model_answer:
(a) A group of living things that can reproduce together to make offspring that can also reproduce.
(b) The short, strong beak can crack hard seeds, so the finch gets food and survives to reproduce.
(c) On each island, finches with the beak best suited to the food there survived and passed on their beak shape. Over a long time the groups became so different that they became new species.
(d) A mutation is a change in a gene. Mutations cause new variation, which natural selection can act on.
marking_scheme:
(a) Can reproduce together to produce fertile offspring (3 marks).
(b) Helps it eat the hard seeds, so it survives and reproduces (3 marks).
(c) Best-suited beaks survive and are passed on; over a long time new species form (3 marks).
(d) A change in a gene (1 mark) + causes variation for natural selection to act on (2 marks).
